Sanders: ‘Medicare for All’ will be HELP priority

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (665 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., holds a news conference in the Capitol on Nov.
  • Saying that “Medicare for All” is no longer “a radical idea,” Sen.
  • Democrats could bring it about through the filibuster-proof budget reconciliation process, the Vermont independent and avowed democratic socialist told reporters.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., holds a news conference in the Capitol on Nov. 10. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

Saying that “Medicare for All” is no longer “a radical idea,” Sen. Bernie Sanders stated Wednesday that he would prioritize passing the universal health care blueprint if he assumes the chairmanship of the Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee next year as expected.

Democrats could bring it about through the filibuster-proof budget reconciliation process, the Vermont independent and avowed democratic socialist told reporters. And the idea could be buoyed by an influx of progressive lawmakers elected in the midterms.

Industry observers note that sanders mentioned Medicare for All is gaining support from voters across the country who are looking to overhaul the American health care system as costs have soared. Democrats on the committee will move the legislation “as aggressively as we can, as rapidly as we can,” he said.

It has been revealed that his version, introduced in April and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, would implement the universal health care system over four years. In the first year, the the age of Medicare eligibility would drop to 55 from 65, while coverage would expand to include dental, hearing and vision care. The bill would also provide coverage for eligible children during the first year.

The age of eligibility would fall another 10 years in each of the following years until the fourth year, when coverage would be extended to all Americans.

In a recent development, “If there has ever been a time in the modern history of our country . . . to address the crises facing working families, this is that time,” Sanders mentioned, noting that Democrats will have a 56-44 majority when the 120th Congress begins in January, the largest margin for either party in 16 years.

Sen. Tammy Baldwin, D-Wis., along with nine other Senate Democrats, last week offered an alternative Medicare expansion blueprint, which would lower the eligibility to those ages 50 and up.

While who will be leading Senate Democrats is still an open question — Chris Van Hollen of Maryland is challenging Charles E. Schumer of Latest York, who has been the top Senate Democrat since 2017 — Sanders remarked he is confident the Medicare for All bill will get to the Senate floor, “no matter who the [Senate majority] leader is.” Sanders previously expressed opposition to Schumer leading the conference.

Asked about efforts to extend the Affordable Care Act enhanced subsidies, Sanders responded he’s “all in.” However, he added “the American people and elected officials understand the current health care system is broken.”.

Subsidies that help enrollees pay for health care premiums on the ACA exchanges were expanded during the COVID-19 pandemic, but these enhanced credits expired at the end of last year, raising costs for many who relied on them to help defray costs.

In a recent development, house Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, nominated on Wednesday to be speaker next year, previously outlined broader health care priorities such as extending the ACA tax credits and reversing Medicaid cuts enacted in Republicans' reconciliation package last year. When asked Tuesday how far Democrats want to lower the Medicare eligibility age, Jeffries responded, “that’s all part of an ongoing conversation.”.

Recent findings suggest that in addition to expanding Medicare coverage, Sanders reiterated his push to lower prescription drug prices. The Vermont lawmaker previously introduced legislation aimed at reducing the cost of brand name prescription drugs by linking domestic prices to international price benchmarks.

To enact some of the agenda, Sanders may have to court Republicans.

Sources indicate that sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., mentioned last week that he prepares to serve as the top Republican on the HELP committee next year. Sanders said Wednesday that his likely GOP counterpart “has shown an enormous amount of courage in taking on Republican leadership year after year.”.

Sanders added that although Paul may have a different viewpoint from himself on committee issues, he looks forward to finding common ground.

#169948. How Much Does A Boeing 737 MAX Pilot Make At Southwest Airlines In 2026?

How Much Does A Boeing 737 MAX Pilot Make At Southwest Airlines In 2026?

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1859 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ask what a Boeing 737 MAX pilot earns at Southwest Airlines, and you can get very different answers from very different sources.
  • What makes Southwest unusual is what happens after the published rate meets the airline's Trip for Pay system, its scheduling practices, and the extra compensation available to pilots who choose to fly more.
  • The airline pays by seat, captain or first officer, and by seniority, under a contract that runs into 2029.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ask what a Boeing 737 MAX pilot earns at Southwest Airlines, and you can get very different answers from very different sources. A captain flying a brand-fresh MAX 8 is paid under the same basic pilot pay system as a colleague flying an older 737-700. The aircraft itself does not create a separate MAX pay scale.

What makes Southwest unusual is what happens after the published rate meets the airline's Trip for Pay system, its scheduling practices, and the extra compensation available to pilots who choose to fly more. Southwest flies only Boeing 737s, so there is no widebody ladder to climb and no separate pay scale for each type.

The airline pays by seat, captain or first officer, and by seniority, under a contract that runs into 2029. In this article, we will walk through the 2026 rates, explain why one hidden multiplier changes the picture, and show how Southwest compares with its rivals. Interestingly, two respected sources read the same pay table in ways that differ by about $51,000 a year.

Industry observers note that the first thing to understand is that the 737 MAX itself has almost nothing to do with the pilot's basic rate. According to Aviation A2Z, the 2026 contract rate runs from $125.90 an hour for a first-year first officer to $240.20 at 12 years, while captains go from $314.76 in their first year to $343.14 at 12 years or more. The same outlet estimates yearly earnings of roughly $82,000 to $285,000 for first officers and $225,000 to $365,000 for captains.

None of those rates change because the pilot is sitting behind the controls of a MAX rather than a 737-700 or 737-800. The more interesting part is what those published rates actually represent. As noted by One Mile at a Time, Southwest operates an all-737 family, so compensation is determined by seat and seniority rather than aircraft variant.

Recent findings suggest that planespotters.net lists 262 737-700s, 188 737-800s and 357 MAX 8s in the fleet, making the MAX the largest single variant. However, there is no separate MAX premium. Wayman's 2026 guide explains why that does not tell the whole story: Southwest uses Trip for Pay, with one TFP representing 243 miles.

Recent findings suggest that as such, the system can produce a much higher effective rate when pilots string together multiple short sectors. The contract itself is the other part of the picture. As reported by the Associated Press via WSVN, about 11,000 Southwest pilots ratified the five-year agreement by a 93% to 7% margin after more than three years of bargaining.

It delivered an immediate 29.15% raise, followed by 4% increases in 2025, 2026 and 2027 and a 3.25% increase in 2028. The 2026 increase is therefore already on the pay scale, while Aviation A2Z says the agreement becomes amendable in January 2029. The question now is how much of that contract rate can actually become a pilot's annual income.

Once the aircraft is taken out of the equation, the Southwest paycheck comes down to seniority, seat, and the amount of credited flying a pilot generates. Aviation A2Z lists $174.48 for a second-year first officer and $217.71 in year five before reaching $240.20 in year 12. Captains begin much higher, at $314.76 in the first year, and reach $343.14 at 12 years or more.

Southwest also contributes 18% non-electively plus 2% through its cash-balance plan in 2026, making retirement benefits an unusually large part of the overall package. The crucial detail is the difference between TFP and conventional block hours. One Mile at a Time notes that Southwest's contract uses a trip-for-pay system, which is why the published figures cannot simply be treated like a conventional airline hourly wage.

Wayman's guide gives a useful illustration: a first-year first officer is listed at an equivalent of $133 per hour, while a 12-year-plus captain reaches $364, with annual estimates based on roughly 75 to 80 credited hours or their TFP equivalent each month. The key word is 'equivalent.' A Southwest pilot can generate more TFP than conventional block-hour calculations would suggest.

Pilot reports on Reddit show just how large that difference can become. One Southwest pilot said he blocked 645 hours in 2025 but was credited with 1,462 TFP, meaning his pay was based on far more credited production than his block time alone would imply. The same pilot said vacation could generate more than 40 TFP for a week and that additional flying could be picked up at 1.5 times or higher.

According to recent reports, another third-year first officer reported just under $300,000 in pure TFP compensation, plus $8,900 in per diem and about $52,000 in 401(k) and similar contributions. Those are individual examples rather than guaranteed earnings, but they explain why Southwest's headline rates can understate what some pilots actually make.

It has been revealed that southwest itself has described the agreement as providing "industry-leading compensation," while union President Casey Murray presented it as the result of prolonged negotiations and pilot solidarity. The Associated Press also placed the deal in the wider pilot-labor market, where airlines have been competing for experienced flight crews.

It has been revealed that this shortage has been particularly notable at smaller carriers, which traditionally provide the experience pipeline for pilots who eventually move to major airlines. The structure of the contract also explains why Southwest's rates look familiar when compared with competitors. One Mile at a Time reported that the negotiated captain rate was tied to Delta's 737 captain rate plus 1%.

Meanwhile, first-officer pay was aligned with Delta's 757 first-officer rate. That arrangement reflects a basic problem for Southwest: its pilots can earn very strong narrowbody compensation, but the airline has no widebody fleet and therefore no larger aircraft to provide the conventional next step after a 737 captain position.

It has been revealed that the contract effectively compensates for that limitation through the negotiated pay scale and other provisions. The labor market remains an crucial part of the story. Simple Flying has reported that the US pilot shortage is not simply a matter of people lacking licenses.

It has been revealed that the harder problem is the supply of experienced captains and the training capacity needed to replace retiring pilots. That environment helped strengthen pilots' bargaining position across the industry. It also makes Southwest's compensation particularly interesting because the airline's unusually productive TFP system can make a strong contract rate translate into substantial real-world earnings.

Comparing Southwest with other airlines requires some care because the most eye-catching numbers often belong to widebody captains. AeroCorner places Southwest ninth in its October 2026 ranking by top captain hourly rate, at roughly $343, compared with $483.74 for 12-year widebody captains at United, American and Delta. That comparison is useful, but it is not a perfect apples-to-apples exercise.

The narrowbody comparison is more revealing. AeroCorner lists JetBlue's A320/A321 captain rate at $359.40 and Alaska's 737 captain rate at $367 or more following its September 2026 increase. Southwest's $343.14 contract figure therefore sits below both when the numbers are compared exactly as published.

First-year first officer (per hour).

$124.72 (before September 2026 raise).

About $343 (737), before 1.149 conversion.

It has been revealed that once the Southwest TFP rate is converted into a block-hour equivalent, however, the comparison changes substantially. That is precisely why published rankings can place Southwest in different positions depending on the methodology used. Southwest does have one striking advantage at the bottom of the seniority ladder.

Specifically, its $125.90 first-year first-officer rate is slightly above United's $125.52 in AeroCorner's comparison and comfortably ahead of JetBlue's $112.32. Once the 18% non-elective retirement contribution and 2% cash-balance contribution are considered, the overall compensation package becomes even more competitive. That does not make Southwest the highest-paying airline in every category, but it does explain why the airline remains an unusually attractive narrowbody job.

According to recent reports, the apparent $51,000 gap comes from comparing two different ways of presenting the same underlying pay rate. The contract figure for a 12-year captain is $343.14, while applying the 1.149 conversion discussed by One Mile at a Time produces an equivalent of about $394.27. If both numbers are simply multiplied by 1,000, the resulting difference is approximately $51,000.

That is a useful illustration of the conversion issue, but it should not be presented as proof that every 12-year Southwest captain actually takes home $394,270 in base pay. Wayman's 2026 guide gives another useful warning against treating an hourly equivalent as a guaranteed annual salary. Its published salary estimates are based on average monthly credited flying.

In a recent development, meanwhile, the guide also notes that senior pilots can exceed the listed figures through profit sharing and premium pay. The Reddit examples point in the same direction. Pilots in the discussion describe vacation credit, additional flying, line-change overrides and higher-paid trips as ways actual compensation can move well beyond a simple base-rate calculation.

Recent findings suggest that one commenter described trips that pay at least 1.5 times the normal rate when they are added under certain circumstances, with some situations reaching two times the normal rate. Delivery timing is another moving part: Simple Flying reported that Southwest and United told Boeing they will not accept latest 737 MAX jets with a recently identified software issue. That may slow new MAX arrivals, though it does not change what pilots are paid.

According to recent reports, so, how much does a Boeing 737 MAX pilot make at Southwest in 2026? The published contract scale runs from $125.90 for a first-year first officer to $343.14 for a 12-year captain, while converting the TFP rates into a block-hour equivalent can produce figures of roughly $145 and $394 respectively. Aviation A2Z's annual estimates run from about $82,000 for a junior first officer to $365,000 for a senior captain.

According to recent reports, wayman's analysis adds another important layer by highlighting the 20% combined retirement contribution, while pilot reports on Reddit show how additional credit and premium flying can push individual compensation substantially higher. The aircraft itself remains the easiest part of the equation. A pilot flying a 737 MAX 8 does not receive a MAX premium simply because the aircraft is newer or has more range than the 737NG.

The MAX's operational advantages can affect Southwest's network, however. As Simple Flying explained, the type's additional range allows Southwest and other carriers to serve markets that would be less practical with earlier 737 generations. That changes where pilots may fly, but it does not create a separate MAX paycheck.

Industry observers note that the next few years will therefore be more interesting for Southwest pilots than the aircraft badge suggests. The 2026 contractual increase is already in effect, another 4% increase is scheduled for 2027, and the final 3.25% increase arrives in 2028, while the agreement becomes amendable in January 2029.

According to recent reports, in 2027, the MAX 7 is also expected to enter Southwest service, adding another 737 variant without creating another pilot pay scale. The real question is how Southwest's TFP system, retirement contributions, premium opportunities, and seniority progression will translate into total compensation as the next contract approaches.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • After close to a year of dire financial warnings, Norway’s Norse Atlantic Airways noted Wednesday that its situation is “critical” and that it must obtain short-term financing to continue operations.
  • The Arendal-based carrier has struggled with higher jet fuel prices brought on by the war in Iran and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
  • “[The organization’s financial condition is] dependent on securing financing to meet its short term liquidity needs and to continue its operations,” officials noted in a statement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After close to a year of dire financial warnings, Norway’s Norse Atlantic Airways noted Wednesday that its situation is “critical” and that it must obtain short-term financing to continue operations.

The Arendal-based carrier has struggled with higher jet fuel prices brought on by the war in Iran and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. In the months since the war started, the airline has cut staff, furloughed some crew members, suspended unprofitable routes, and instituted temporary pay reductions for some non-flying crew, but these steps have apparently not put Norse Atlantic back on solid ground.

“[The organization’s financial condition is] dependent on securing financing to meet its short term liquidity needs and to continue its operations,” officials noted in a statement. “Norse, supported by its advisors, has explored various strategic alternatives and entertains discussions for a potential takeover.”.

“Norse is also engaged in discussions with selected parties on short term financing, however, there can be no assurances that such discussions will result in a viable solution,” the message continued. “Norse will provide further information as and when appropriate.”.

Rising fuel costs have set back airlines around the world, but the squeeze is arguably worst in Europe, since the continent depends mainly on Gulf oil and has little domestic refining capacity. The crisis has forced Latvia’s airBaltic into bankruptcy, teed up EasyJet’s sale to Apollo Global Management, and inflicted considerable damage on Lufthansa’s core brand.

Sources indicate that it was not immediately clear if Norse Atlantic has any candidates in mind for a potential merger. The carrier is not part of any global airline alliance, though it partners with operators such as EasyJet, Norwegian Air Shuttle, and Pegasus through its Norse Connections program.

Bloomberg reported in 2023 and 2024 that the carrier was weighing alliances with larger airlines, possibly through an equity stake, but none were named.

Sources indicate that norse Atlantic operates only long-haul flights. Its network has been adjusted multiple times over the last year in an effort to reduce costs.

The Real Reason Why Boeing Never Believed In Gear Doors For Its Best-Selling Jet

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1464 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In 1958, Boeing debuted the 707, which was its first jet airliner, and the aircraft promptly became a huge success.
  • According to recent reports, as all three were narrowbodies, they shared some common fuselage design elements, but were otherwise very different from one another given their different intended missions.
  • The 727's MLG has two wheels, which are stowed in a covered gear bay in flight.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In 1958, Boeing debuted the 707, which was its first jet airliner, and the aircraft promptly became a huge success. Following the popularity of the large, long-range 707, the 727, a mid-size, mid-range aircraft, entered service in 1964. In 1968, the 737, which was an even smaller aircraft designed for short-haul routes, entered service.

According to recent reports, as all three were narrowbodies, they shared some common fuselage design elements, but were otherwise very different from one another given their different intended missions. One key difference between the three aircraft is their landing gear. The 707's main landing gear (MLG) design features four wheels, retracting in a gear bay covered by doors.

The 727's MLG has two wheels, which are stowed in a covered gear bay in flight. The 737's MLG features two wheels, but uniquely, the sides of the tires are exposed in flight, as the 737 does not have large gear bay doors that fully cover the MLG. Interestingly, this isn't particularly unusual with narrowbody airliners.

Sources indicate that boeing originally designed the 737 with exposed MLG back in the 1960s, and this design has persisted ever since because designing a upcoming MLG for the 737 would be enormously complicated and expensive. In the 1960s, the 737 was expected to operate mainly to small, underdeveloped airfields, and this MLG design would simplify line maintenance at these outstations.

Recent findings suggest that today, however, modern 737s are large mainline aircraft, and this is no longer a concern for most 737 operators. While the benefit of simplified maintenance at underdeveloped outstations is less of a prominent factor today, there are other benefits. Since the aircraft doesn't need a complex door mechanism, the MLG system is simpler, reducing costs.

In addition, omitting an MLG gear bay door system reduces weight, lowering fuel burn. While this design is less aerodynamic, the 737 features rubber seals around the bottom of the wheel wells, smaller doors covering the gear struts, and hubcaps on the outer wheels. These design elements reduce the drag impact of the exposed gear bays, although they remain less aerodynamic and noisier than an MLG bay with doors.

Still, the entire design is lighter and less complex than one with gear bay doors, which are strong benefits. On shorter flights, such as those that the 737 was originally intended to operate, the benefits of the exposed MLG can actually outweigh the drag penalty, which is why several other short-range aircraft have exposed gear bays.

There is rarely one 'single' answer in aircraft design, as each choice comes with benefits and drawbacks that need to be considered during development. Notably, the 737's initial competitor, the McDonnell Douglas DC-9, did feature gear bay doors, while the later Airbus A320 also features gear bay doors.

However, while fully enclosed doors were considered the better option for the DC-9 and A320, this doesn't actually mean that the 737 would have benefited from them even in its modern, longer-range form today. The aircraft's general intended mission plays a role; on shorter flights, the drag impact of the exposed wheels has less of an impact than on longer services.

Another part, however, has to do with the overall aerodynamic profile of the aircraft. Depending on where air is actually flowing around the 737's airframe and wings, there may have been less of an aerodynamic benefit to moving to covered gear bay doors, compared to doing the same for the DC-9 or A320. Of course, only Boeing knows the full benefit of the exposed gear bays on the 737.

Recent findings suggest that while the 737 Classic has more similarities with the original 737, the 737NG received an all-new wing and wingbox design. It would have been easier to integrate landing gear doors than in the past, but Boeing still opted to omit them. Not only would MLG doors add weight and increase maintenance costs, but they can end up increasing the size of the belly fairing depending on how the aircraft has been designed overall. This could result in more drag overall with the 737, offsetting any benefits.

In the short-haul world, covered gear bay doors are not nearly as uncommon as one might imagine. The Embraer ERJ and Bombardier CRJ lines also feature exposed gear bay doors, while being much newer designs than the 737. They are also small regional jets mainly used for short-haul flights.

Recent findings suggest that many small business jets are designed with exposed gear doors, although these do tend to operate shorter flights than even what a modern 737 operates. The same is also true for the ATR 42 and ATR 72. Rather interestingly, exposed wheel wells have actually been fairly popular with small aircraft in recent years.

According to recent reports, while the 727, DC-9, BAC One-Eleven, and A320 have MLG doors, the even newer Embraer E-Jet series does not, while the succeeding E2 does. Furthermore, the Airbus A220 has exposed landing gear. The A220 is the newest Western aircraft type in service today, and it has the range to operate routes as long as US transcontinental services, yet Bombardier (the original designer of the A220) omitted gear bay doors.

In a recent development, landing gear bay doors are usually more aerodynamic on their own than using exposed main landing gear, but they also add weight and complexity. The weight savings from using an exposed MLG design can be much more consequential for a smaller aircraft type, and, notably, modern 737s are among the largest commercial airliners to use an exposed design. Of course, this hardly means exposed landing gear is necessarily a competitive design choice for all aircraft types.

The 737 is Boeing's only commercial jet airliner with exposed MLG bays. The later 757 has covered gear bays, while all of Airbus's aircraft feature gear bay doors. All of McDonnell Douglas's commercial jetliners feature gear bay doors as well. Depending on how the aircraft is designed, the aerodynamic benefits of the MLG doors may be greater than the weight savings.

Recent findings suggest that various elements of the aircraft's design also factor into whether the plane would be better with exposed gear or bay doors. Larger aircraft, ranging from the 757 to widebodies like the 787, have at least four wheels per MLG bogey, and exposing all four wheels would prove impractical due to the size and complexity of the MLG bogeys.

Airbus A220 (Bombardier CSeries).

​​​​​​​This is why essentially every airliner with four wheels or more per MLG bogey has gear doors. In addition, the aerodynamic benefits of MLG doors are more pronounced on longer routes, while larger, heavier planes feel less of an impact from the weight savings offered by exposed wheel wells. Perhaps the most interesting contrast is with the A320, which is the direct rival to modern 737 variants.

It has been revealed that the A320's gear bay doors are heavier but more aerodynamic. What's curious here is that the different variants of the A320 are sized very close to the 737, and these aircraft also have similar range, operating flights of very similar length. As a whole, they deliver very similar results for airlines and have very similar capabilities, but they take different approaches to get there.

The A320 type is about 20 years younger than the original 737, and it therefore has an aerodynamic profile much newer than its Boeing rival. Notably, however, the modern A320 is still using largely the same wing as what Airbus originally designed in the late 1980s. The 737 received a new wing in the late 1990s, when Boeing developed the 737NG.

This means that the 737 MAX, which has largely the same wing design as the 737NG, actually has a newer, larger wing than the A320neo. The A320 is more technologically advanced than the 737, while one long-standing advantage of the 737 against the A320 has been its lower weight, helping fuel burn. The 737-800 in particular actually seats slightly more passengers than the competing A320-200, while also having slightly more range.

As such, it's slightly outsold the A320-200, while the A319-100 slightly outsold the 737-700. The A321-200 significantly outsold the competing 737-900 and 737-900ER as it's significantly larger and more economical. With the latest 737 MAX and A320neo families, the 737 MAX has actually gained slightly more weight compared to the A320neo due to the latest engines.

Sources indicate that the 737 MAX tends to burn less fuel during climb, while the A320neo family is reportedly more efficient during cruise, making it better for long-range routes. The 737 MAX 8 has remained extremely popular, but the A321neo has become a runaway success due to its range and economics, which Boeing has only recently been able to compete effectively against with the slightly lighter-weight 737 MAX 10.

    Lawmakers Criticize FAA Deploying Upcoming “Untested” AI Tool Days Before Nationwide Grounding

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (877 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that A group of 24 Democratic lawmakers has criticized the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) for prematurely deploying a new artificial intelligence (AI) tool across US airspace.
    • According to recent reports, the nationwide deployment of the Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes, and Trajectories (SMART) system came just three days before a telecommunications failure brought US departures to a standstill.
    • Recent findings suggest that led by House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee Ranking Member Rick Larsen, the lawmakers allege that the FAA expanded the SMART system nationwide without notifying Congress in advance.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that A group of 24 Democratic lawmakers has criticized the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) for prematurely deploying a new artificial intelligence (AI) tool across US airspace. In a letter to FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford on Tuesday, the lawmakers accused the agency of expanding a largely untested system nationwide before completing its promised 90-day validation period.

    According to recent reports, the nationwide deployment of the Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes, and Trajectories (SMART) system came just three days before a telecommunications failure brought US departures to a standstill. While the FAA has denied any connection between the two events, the controversy raises fresh questions about whether the Trump administration's ambitious air traffic control (ATC) modernization program is prioritizing the speed of implementation over adequate testing, safety oversight, and transparency.

    Recent findings suggest that led by House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee Ranking Member Rick Larsen, the lawmakers allege that the FAA expanded the SMART system nationwide without notifying Congress in advance. The expansion came just 50 days after its initial deployment in the Washington area, despite the FAA previously outlining a 90-day validation period.

    In their letter to Bedford, the lawmakers expressed frustration with the lack of supporting safety data.

    “We have yet to receive any substantive information proving the system was properly validated before its nationwide expansion.”.

    Concerns surrounding SMART considerably predate the nationwide grounding. In September, the National Air Traffic Controllers Association (NATCA) told Flying Magazine that it had been excluded from the system's development, testing, and implementation. Lawmakers subsequently requested that the FAA suspend SMART operations and called for an independent Government Accountability Office (GAO) audit. More troublingly, the latest letter cites allegations that FAA employees who raised safety concerns about SMART's accelerated deployment may have faced retaliation.

    FAA awards $875 million SMART contract.

    Airline industry concerns emerge.

    SMART launches at three Washington-area airports.

    NATCA's exclusion from development and testing is reported.

    Lawmakers request suspension of SMART operations.

    Congressional request for an independent GAO audit.

    SMART expands to all 22 enroute control centers.

    24 House Democrats demand answers from FAA.

    FAA and DOT officials scheduled to testify before Congress.

    The lawmakers have presented the FAA with 13 questions, demanding details on its safety assessments, performance metrics, controller training, cybersecurity protections, and contingency looks if SMART experiences an outage. They also question why the agency prioritized deploying SMART over essential infrastructure upgrades, including radar replacements. Reuters reported that the FAA has declined to address the allegations publicly, saying it will respond directly to lawmakers.

    Developed by Air Space Intelligence (ASI) under an $875 million, 12-year contract, SMART is designed to make the increasingly congested US airspace more efficient. The cloud-based technology consolidates approximately 200 data streams, encompassing weather forecasts, flight trajectories, airport capacity, and controller staffing. Its predictive capabilities allow aviation professionals to anticipate operational bottlenecks and identify alternative flight paths before disruptions materialize.

    Importantly, SMART does not autonomously direct aircraft. FAA specialists at a dedicated center in Washington review its recommendations before forwarding them to the agency's Air Traffic Control System Command Center in Warrenton, Virginia. Human controllers retain ultimate operational authority. The technology is similar to ASI's Flyways AI platform, which Alaska Airlines began using in 2021 to help flight dispatchers optimize aircraft routing.

    Time before nationwide expansion.

    En-route control centers covered.

    Flights rerouted during initial rollout.

    Average time saved per rerouted flight.

    Average fuel saved per rerouted flight.

    The potential commercial benefits are substantial, and United Airlines, Delta Air Lines, American Airlines, and Southwest Airlines have all expressed support for the initiative. According to the FAA, and as reported by Aerotime, SMART's initial deployment delivered measurable efficiency improvements, potentially translating into considerable fuel savings and fewer passenger disruptions when replicated nationally. However, lawmakers argue that evidence of improved operational efficiency cannot substitute for comprehensive safety validation.

    Recent findings suggest that the concerns come amid the shock of the November 13 nationwide ground stop, which demonstrated the vulnerability of America's existing ATC infrastructure. The FAA's preliminary investigation identified a telecommunications failure, with excessive data traffic overwhelming legacy equipment following routine maintenance work. The resulting instability affected communications and radar feeds across much of the country. Both the FAA and ASI have explicitly denied that SMART contributed to the disruption.

    November 13 Nationwide Ground Stop.

    Enroute control centers affected.

    Airborne aircraft safely landed.

    Total flight cancellations on November 13.

    Cancellations across the wider disruption.

    The incident was the first nationwide ground stop since the January 2023 failure of the FAA's NOTAM system. A September 2026 GAO report highlighted significant shortcomings in the FAA's modernization cost estimates and scheduling. Previous research found that 105 of the agency's 138 ATC systems were either unsustainable or potentially unsustainable, illustrating the urgency of replacing aging infrastructure while maintaining the integrity of existing operations.

    Congressional scrutiny is set to intensify next week, with Bedford expected to appear before a House panel on December 1 and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy scheduled to testify before the Senate on December 2. Duffy's request for approximately $50 billion in additional aviation infrastructure funding, including $600 million for strategic traffic flow management technologies such as SMART, already faces significant opposition. Securing that funding may increasingly depend on the FAA demonstrating that its accelerated modernization efforts are not compromising safety.

    The deal is Boeing’s largest with a Chinese operator in nearly a decade. The country largely shifted toward Airbus aircraft as relations with the U.S. frayed.

    President Donald Trump hoped to reverse that trend during his state visit to China in May. Trump discussed a potential purchase directly with Chinese President Xi Jinping, and even brought along Boeing CEO Kelly Ortberg for the summit. Ultimately, Beijing agreed to buy 200 aircraft from Boeing, fewer than analysts expected, but still notable considering Boeing’s drought in the country.

    Trump stated earlier this week that he thinks China will buy 250 more aircraft from Boeing. He did not provide details or say where that information came from.

    China Southern mentioned the upcoming aircraft will help Xiamen expand after it relocates to the new Xiamen Xiang’an International Airport. The facility will replace Xiamen Gaoqi International Airport as Xiamen’s main gateway.

    #169937. How Much Does A Rolls-Royce Trent 1000 Engine Cost?

    📅 28 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1585 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Simpleflying ↗ Open Full Page

    How Much Does A Rolls-Royce Trent 1000 Engine Cost?

    📅 28 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1585 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that rolls-Royce does not publish list prices for the Trent 1000, so every figure quoted for the Dreamliner engine is an estimate, and the most commonly cited is about $20 million per engine.
    • A better answer therefore separates three prices: what an engine is estimated to cost at list, what a documented order implies once its fine print is read, and what it costs to keep one flying.
    • Simple Flying’s 2025 survey of commercial engines places the Trent 1000 at an estimated $20 million, which sits below the roughly $22 million it assigns to the rival GE GEnx and well below Rolls-Royce’s own Trent 7000 at $25 million and Trent XWB at $35 million.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that rolls-Royce does not publish list prices for the Trent 1000, so every figure quoted for the Dreamliner engine is an estimate, and the most commonly cited is about $20 million per engine. That number answers only part of the question, because transaction prices differ from list estimates and the expense that has defined this engine’s reputation arrives years after delivery in the form of shop visits and retrofit campaigns.

    A better answer therefore separates three prices: what an engine is estimated to cost at list, what a documented order implies once its fine print is read, and what it costs to keep one flying. This article works through each, then examines how Rolls-Royce’s latest upgrade could change the ownership economics.

    Simple Flying’s 2025 survey of commercial engines places the Trent 1000 at an estimated $20 million, which sits below the roughly $22 million it assigns to the rival GE GEnx and well below Rolls-Royce’s own Trent 7000 at $25 million and Trent XWB at $35 million. The Trent 1000 can reach 74,411 pounds of thrust (331 kN), and the Trent 7000’s thrust band falls within that limit as well, so thrust alone does not explain the price spread. SlashGear arrives at the same $20 million figure and describes an engine optimized for the Boeing 787, with a fan that produces about 85% of the engine’s total thrust.

    These figures are best read as list-price approximations rather than transaction prices, since common estimates exclude discounts, bulk purchase pricing, and support contracts. For example, Singapore Airlines had an order for 62 GE9X engines with a list value of about $45 million per engine, including a 12-year service contract. For context, narrowbody engines are not necessarily cheaper once transactions replace estimates: Willis Lease Finance purchased 15 Pratt & Whitney PW1100 engines in 2024 for $363.9 million, about $24.3 million each, more than the Trent 1000 estimate.

    Recent findings suggest that the clearest official data point is a January 2018 announcement in which Rolls-Royce mentioned lessor AerCap had ordered Trent 1000 engines to power 10 Boeing 787s, a deal valued at $450 million at list prices. Dividing by 20 engines yields $22.5 million apiece, the figure usually quoted, but the arithmetic depends on assumptions the announcement does not confirm: two engines per aircraft and no spares.

    A footnote in the release adds a more significant caveat, since Rolls-Royce measures its order book at list prices and, for long-term aftermarket contracts, counts the revenue it expects to recognize within seven years of the announcement. The release does not say whether such revenue sits inside the $450 million, so the $22.5 million figure may blend hardware with service value and should be treated as an upper reference for the engine itself rather than a price tag. The footnote also cautions that an order’s stated value may not reflect future revenue.

    Industry observers note that two other details bound the interpretation, since the order covered the TEN variant, which entered service in November 2017, and AerCap held options on five more aircraft outside the stated value. The TEN draws on Trent XWB and Advance technologies and helps the Dreamliner achieve 20% greater efficiency than the aircraft it replaces, according to Rolls-Royce. Rolls-Royce also notes that the Trent 1000 powered the first flight of every Dreamliner version, the 787-8, 787-9, and 787-10. Because list prices exclude negotiated discounts, the price AerCap actually paid is not disclosed in the announcement.

    Tada Images | Shutterstock, Simple Flying.

    According to recent reports, purchase price is only the entry fee, because Simple Flying reports that a single unscheduled shop visit can exceed $5 million once transport logistics, spare engine leasing, and teardown labor are counted. The same report states early Trent 1000s achieved time-on-wing intervals that were a fraction of the GEnx-1B benchmark of more than 20,000 operating hours before the first major shop visit, which made the interval the main driver of lifetime cost. Because the Trent 1000 is a three-shaft design built exclusively for the Dreamliner, its tooling, spare parts, and overhaul procedures are unique to it and are not shared with the GEnx fleet.

    Many Rolls-Royce operators shield themselves from that volatility through TotalCare, a power-by-the-hour agreement in which the airline pays a fixed rate per flight hour and the manufacturer assumes the cost of shop visits. Such contracts convert an uncertain maintenance expense into a predictable one, though the engine’s true cost to the operator then becomes a recurring rate rather than a single purchase price. Because the fleet now spans several build standards, airlines and maintenance hubs must also manage parts inventories and tooling for each sub-generation, an overhead that TotalCare terms do not remove.

    Industry observers note that rolls-Royce’s exposure under those agreements explains why durability failures hurt it directly: in 2019, the organization stated added repair costs would push a small number of its contracts into loss-making territory, which its finance chief put at around three. Those losses made up about half of an exceptional charge of about £1.4 billion expected that year.

    Wikimedia Commons | Simple Flying.

    The technical cause was corrosion-related fatigue cracking in the intermediate- and high-pressure turbine blades, which emerged within five years of the engine’s 2011 entry into service and eventually affected as many as 500 engines. Groundings peaked at close to 50 Dreamliners in 2018, and in April of that year the FAA cut extended-range twin-engine operating time for Package C aircraft from 330 minutes to 140, a restriction that complicated long trans-Pacific planning. Operators such as Air Latest Zealand and British Airways grounded aircraft for inspections, and several affected carriers leased older, less fuel-efficient jets to protect schedules, which added millions of dollars in operating expense.

    According to recent reports, the financial tally has grown with each revision: by November 2019, Rolls-Royce put the cost of the Trent 1000 problems at £2.4 billion for 2017 through 2023, an additional £800 million, and said the TEN would need servicing every four years instead of five. Later accounts place the total above $3 billion, covering retrofits, engine modifications, and customer compensation.

    The commercial damage extended beyond Rolls-Royce’s accounts, as GE secured roughly two-thirds of the in-service 787 fleet and recent widebody sales campaigns ordered 677 GEnx-powered aircraft against only 71 for the Trent 1000. Emirates President Tim Clark, citing instability in the Trent program, noted in September 2019 that he would not commit to ordering 787s, an early sign that reliability concerns could cost sales as well as repair money.

    Sources indicate that rolls-Royce’s answer is the Trent 1000 XE, delivered in two certified phases; the first, approved by the FAA in June 2025, introduced a high-pressure turbine blade with 40% more cooling, along with changes to the combustor, fuel spray nozzles, and controller software. Rolls-Royce claims that package alone more than doubles the time on wing, and the second phase, certified in late 2025, redesigns the blade shroud and adds advanced coatings for roughly 30% more. Together, the phases are meant to triple time on wing relative to the TEN, and CEO Tufan Erginbilgiç has put the real-world figure as high as six years between shop visits for some customers. The confidence rests partly on the Trent 7000, which has flown with the same durability technology since 2022, and by mid-2026 the fleet using the new blades had accumulated almost three million engine flying hours.

    Deployment is under way, since Lufthansa flew the first XE-equipped 787 in November 2025. The XE is now standard on upcoming Trent-powered deliveries, and by early 2026, more than 50 in-service engines carried the improved blades, with a fleet-wide retrofit targeted for the end of 2027. Rolls-Royce committed to upgrading existing engines at no additional charge to airlines, and it added maintenance capacity in the UK, Germany, and Singapore worth roughly 100 more shop visits a year. LATAM Airlines has selected the XE for its 787s, a win Rolls-Royce credits to the durability gains.

    The Trent 1000 work forms part of a £1 billion durability program that also covers the Trent 7000 and Trent XWB, and Rolls-Royce has raised its mid-term time-on-wing improvement target from 40% to 80% by 2027. Investors reacted by pushing Rolls-Royce shares sharply higher after the tech giant raised its profit guidance on the back of the engine fixes.

    Over the next two years, the price tag on a Trent 1000 will likely matter less than evidence of how long upgraded engines stay on wing. Once the fleet retrofit concludes, the industry will have its first fleet-scale record of shop visit intervals for the XE standard, and that record should do more than any list estimate to set how lessors and operators value the engine. Simple arithmetic demonstrates why, since tripling the interval between visits would cut visits per flying hour to about a third, a change in lifetime economics that outweighs the small purchase price gap separating the Trent 1000 from its GE rival.

    Two uncertainties remain, since the sources reviewed do not say whether the XE standard changes the purchase price of a new engine, and the headline interval claims apply to some customers rather than the whole fleet. Pricing is therefore likely to shift toward service contract terms, where Rolls-Royce can back its durability claims with guaranteed rates, and away from the hardware figure that dominates headlines. If the 2027 data confirm the promised gains, the engine’s share of new 787 orders will be the first place the market shows that it believes them.

    • The day after Alexander Calder presented his initiative for a public art display in the Hart Building’s nine-story atrium to the Architect of the Capitol, he died.
    • It has been revealed that fifty years later, Alexander S.C.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sen. Alex Padilla, D-Calif., speaks during a ceremony marking the restoration of Alexander Calder’s Mountains and Clouds sculpture in the Hart Senate Office Building atrium on Wednesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

    The day after Alexander Calder presented his initiative for a public art display in the Hart Building’s nine-story atrium to the Architect of the Capitol, he died.

    It has been revealed that fifty years later, Alexander S.C. Rower felt a sense of awe as he stared up at his grandfather’s work, finally restored to what he had envisioned.

    Sources indicate that “It’s totally phenomenal,” he noted, pointing up at the now-moving clouds as he spoke, spinning his finger around. “It’s not entertainment, but it’s trying to emulate naturalness, trying to emulate what nature would do.”.

    It was a long time coming for Rower, who remembers traveling to the Capitol in his 20s for the original dedication of the Mountains and Clouds sculpture in 1987. The mobile portion stopped rotating as Calder intended in the 1990s, and it was ultimately removed in 2014 after being deemed unsafe by the Architect of the Capitol. Millions of dollars in private philanthropy later, Calder’s clouds are spinning again.

    Rower was back on the Hill on Wednesday for an event celebrating the restoration, joining Architect of the Capitol Thomas Austin, Sens. Alex Padilla, D-Calif., Angus King, I-Maine, and James Lankford, R-Okla., and the project’s donors. As the speakers addressed the crowd, the clouds began to speed up slightly. Onlookers gathered on the balconies overlooking the atrium and peeked through office windows. Attendees left with tote bags emblazoned with images of Calder’s art.

    According to Rower, who leads the Calder Foundation dedicated to preserving and interpreting his grandfather’s art, the mobile is rotating on a 15-hour cycle that is “totally variable.”.

    Industry observers note that “It can go a little faster; it can go a little slower,” he said. “I told the team today that during lunchtime, I want it to speed up just a little bit because everyone’s going to lunch. There’ll be … a lot of activity passing through, and then right at 2:30, well, let’s make it go quieter.”.

    It was a labor of love for those involved, and not an inexpensive one. Jon and Kim Shirley funded the $12 million restoration. Because the pieces were so large, they were transported on an extra-wide load truck and driven at a speed of 35 miles per hour from Michigan.

    “We had to call every senator or governor that we knew on that route, which went through seven states, to get permissions,” he mentioned. “That was a huge thing to overcome, and it all happened over a weekend. So my wife was actually on the phone with a governor’s wife on Saturday evening. The next day, he called up his Department of Transportation and got a permit.”.

    Christian Quilici, who helped manage the project on behalf of the Shirleys and said he serves as a liaison between the foundation and Congress, said the hardest part of the project was the size of it.

    Industry observers note that “We had to tear the wall down on C Street, which nobody really thought of in the beginning,” he said. “Nobody got how big this was until it showed up on their doorstep.”.

    Industry observers note that quilici said he spent years educating at least 30 different senators about the quest to reunite the mobile with the stationary mountains left behind. Some of the biggest champions were seated in the front row at Wednesday’s event, including Senate Democratic Whip Richard J. Durbin. Absent was Sen. Christopher S. Murphy, D-Conn., who has been away from the Capitol while recovering from a stroke but has been a supporter of the sculpture’s restoration for years, pressing former acting Architect of the Capitol Joseph DiPietro on it at a 2024 Senate Legislative Branch Appropriations budget hearing.

    “Is there any chance that before I leave the Senate, or at least before I die, we can get the clouds back up there?” Murphy said at the time.

    Padilla read a letter on Wednesday from Murphy, whose state was Calder’s home for much of his life.

    Industry observers note that “This statue is actually a statement on our democracy, that we have substantial pieces of monumental art right in the middle of our most notable and most iconic government buildings. To get this piece of art restored to how it was designed by the artist, well, that’s good for Connecticut. But I also like to think … it’s good for democracy too,” Murphy’s statement remarked.

    The restoration was funded entirely by donations from the Shirleys, who are prominent Calder collectors, according to Rower.

    It has been revealed that “It’s very emotional to see the work completed after 10 years of us working so hard with the Architect of the Capitol and Calder Foundation. It’s a very overpowering, overwhelming emotion,” remarked Kim Shirley.

    Sources indicate that in addition to helping fund the project, she’s a former Senate staffer who worked in Hart before Calder’s work was installed. Years after her time in the Senate was over, her husband Jon wanted to show her the sculpture, now filling the space she used to walk through every day.

    Industry observers note that but when the two arrived, the clouds weren’t hanging from the ceiling like they were supposed to be. He called up Rower, who was a friend of his, and mentioned he wanted to get them back to how Calder intended. On Wednesday, the three of them stood together in Hart, looking up.

    Technological and engineering advancements allowed for newer, lighter clouds to be built and be safe to hang from the ceiling.

    “Before it was like a bulb, it looked like a hoagie sandwich, and now it looks just really sharp, like a razor cutting through space, which was Calder’s intention,” Rower said.

    According to Rower, it involved laser-measuring the original model of Mountains and Clouds sitting in a glass case nearby in the Hart atrium. The upcoming clouds, he remarked, are made of carbon fiber.

    “These are giant things up in the air, and they’re just so gentle and subtle,” he noted.

    In a recent development, younger Hill staffers don’t know a time with clouds. But for those who have spent decades in the building, it was a special moment to see them spin, as Lankford told the crowd.

    “I can’t tell you how many tour groups that I’ve walked through this building and I pointed to this, and I stated it’s only half there, and would take them over to the little model that’s right over here, and say this is what it’s supposed to look like,” said the senator, a former Hill staffer himself.

    Standing under his grandfather’s sculpture, Rower found himself quoting the man responsible for it all.

    “I find that everything I do, if it is made for a particular spot, is more successful,” he mentioned, gazing up at it.

    • But with a little planning, you can make the most of your credit card rewards and benefits without overspending.
    • Here are five tips to help you save money and earn rewards like a pro this holiday season.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Although the holiday season can be joyous, it can be an expensive time of year, with gifts, travel and gatherings putting extra pressure on your budget.

    But with a little planning, you can make the most of your credit card rewards and benefits without overspending.

    Here are five tips to help you save money and earn rewards like a pro this holiday season.

    According to recent reports, first, map out your holiday shopping looks and set a realistic budget for spending. Who are you shopping for? How much are you planning to spend on gifts? What other expenses should you factor into your holiday budget?

    These are all good questions to help you set expectations and prevent impulse buys that can lead to overspending.

    A spreadsheet is a great way to keep track of spending and budgeting. You can simply insert your budget into a premade template or write it down on paper. If you already know what you proposal to buy, insert links to the sales pages so you know how much it will cost.

    While adjusting and finalizing your budget, remember to factor in additional costs due to extra gatherings, like larger grocery and dining expenses.

    One of the best things about rewards cards is that they often come with perks to help you save money.

    Before making your holiday purchases, check whether your credit cards offer statement credits or other benefits that could help you save money.

    In a recent development, for example, comes with an up to $75 quarterly statement credit (up to $300 annually) Lululemon credit that can be used at U.S. stores (excluding outlets) or online after enrollment. This is a great way to maximize purchases on clothing, yoga gear or other accessories.

    Or, if you have a frequent jet-setter in your life, you can use a credit card’s Global Entry/TSA PreCheck credit to cover their application fee of up to $120.

    Sources indicate that statement credits aren't the only card benefits worth checking before you shop. For an expensive electronic device or other high-value gift, purchase protection or extended warranty coverage are other useful perks.

    We talk a lot about shopping portals during this time of year. That's because skipping them is essentially leaving money on the table.

    According to recent reports, by doing your online holiday shopping through a portal, you can earn bonus points or cash back at a massive number of online retailers. Most of the major U.S. airlines have shopping portals to help you earn additional miles on every eligible purchase, or you can use third-party portals such as Rakuten to earn cash back or Amex Membership Rewards or Bilt Points.

    We suggest using a shopping portal aggregator like Cashback Monitor to find the best portal for each online purchase. That way, you don’t have to sift through each portal’s offers individually.

    No matter where you shop, review any Amex Offers, Chase Offers or Citi Merchant Offers available on your cards. They vary by cardmember, and often stack with your card's standard rewards plus a shopping portal. Some require activation or enrollment before making a purchase.

    Related: Everything you need to know about credit card merchant offers.

    It has been revealed that we’re significant fans of points and miles at The Points Guy — and for good reason. Points and miles can reduce the cost of future travel, but cash-back cards may be more useful if you want rewards to offset your holiday expenses directly.

    A flat-rate cash-back card such as the (see rates and fees) is an easy way to earn rewards no matter where you shop since it offers 1% cash back when you make a purchase and another 1% cash back when you pay your bill. Redeeming those rewards as a statement credit helps reduce the size of January's bill.

    The (see rates and fees) is another great option that earns at least 1.5% back on every purchase.

    Related: Best cash-back credit cards.

    Paying your statement balance in full is generally best, but some rewards credit cards offer a 0% introductory annual percentage rate period on fresh purchases. That can give you time to pay for a planned expense without interest as long as you have a plan to pay it off completely before the introductory period ends.

    According to recent reports, another option is to use one of the financing options some credit card issuers offer. Amex Initiative It® and Chase Pay Over Time after purchase may allow eligible cardmembers to divide qualifying purchases of $100 or more into fixed monthly payments, generally with a fixed monthly fee instead of interest.

    You’ll almost always save money using these programs compared to paying interest over time.

    Related: Chase Pay Over Time and My Chase Loan: Should you opt in?

    Sources indicate that holiday shopping doesn't have to derail your budget. By planning ahead, using the right rewards cards and taking advantage of statement credits and shopping portals, you can make your spending more rewarding without buying more than you can afford.

    The key is to prioritize your budget over earning points, miles or cash back. After all, the value of those rewards can promptly disappear if you're carrying a balance and paying interest.

    #169932. The Airbus A380 Burns Over 3,000 Gallons An Hour & Still Pays Off For Emirates

    📅 28 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1533 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Simpleflying ↗ Open Full Page

    The Airbus A380 Burns Over 3,000 Gallons An Hour & Still Pays Off For Emirates

    📅 28 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1533 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that the Airbus A380 burns far more than 3,000 gallons (approximately 11,356 liters) of fuel every single hour, significantly higher than what would be expected from a modern widebody aircraft.
    • In a recent development, how can an airframe that consumes thousands of gallons per hour still pay off when other airlines view it as a commercial liability?
    • On an hourly basis, the A380's fuel consumption stands out immediately against modern twin-engine long-haul aircraft.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that the Airbus A380 burns far more than 3,000 gallons (approximately 11,356 liters) of fuel every single hour, significantly higher than what would be expected from a modern widebody aircraft. Despite the high figure, Emirates keeps the four-engine superjumbo central to its long-haul network. Across the wider airline industry, most carriers have scaled back, parked, or retired their double-deckers because four engines bring steep fuel burn and heavy maintenance demands on ordinary routes. Emirates has defied this trend and continues to fly the aircraft across major global trunk routes, honing the high hourly consumption into a core element of its commercial strategy.

    In a recent development, how can an airframe that consumes thousands of gallons per hour still pay off when other airlines view it as a commercial liability? Success ultimately comes from filling hundreds of seats on flights into slot-constrained airports backed by strong connecting hub traffic. Looking closely at the A380's fuel burn, per-seat economics, hub advantages, financial track record, and future outlook, it becomes clear that the type still makes sense for Emirates.

    On an hourly basis, the A380's fuel consumption stands out immediately against modern twin-engine long-haul aircraft. Figures cited by Simple Flying place the A380's fuel burn at roughly 4,600 gallons (approximately 17,413 liters) per hour, nearly double the roughly 2,700 gallons (approximately 10,221 liters) per hour burned by an Airbus A350-1000. That wide gap stems from four large turbofans moving a heavier double-deck airframe across long sectors, where takeoff weight, cruise altitude, headwinds, and route length continually shape exact hourly consumption.

    According to recent reports, emirates President Tim Clark has framed that hourly fuel burn in weight terms as well as volume, as noted by Airline Ratings. On a long-haul flight from Dubai International Airport (DXB) to Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) carrying 515 passengers, Clark has indicated that fuel burn runs around 13 tonnes (approximately 28,660 pounds) per hour. Across the full trip between the two hubs, total fuel burn reaches roughly 200 tonnes (approximately 440,925 pounds).

    In a recent development, those figures show why the A380 looks daunting whenever an airline evaluates raw fuel burn in isolation rather than total seat capacity. Burning that much fuel every hour creates a substantial fuel bill on paper, which will naturally lead most airlines to look elsewhere for widebody capacity. With that in mind, it seems somewhat nonsensical for Emirates to stick with the A380 when all its rivals have ceded to the extortionate costs.

    In a recent development, once fuel burn is divided across hundreds of seats, not just being viewed purely per hour, the A380's commercial math changes sharply. Using the Dubai-to-Los Angeles comparison noted by AirlineRatings, Emirates President Tim Clark has explained that the A380's fuel cost per seat can beat running two Boeing 787 flights, each of which burns roughly half as much fuel as the superjumbo. That advantage holds when high load factors keep cabins well filled, whereas flying a large double-decker with dozens of empty seats quickly destroys per-passenger efficiency.

    Slot-constrained airports turn that high seat count into an even bigger practical asset on trunk routes. As The Economist reports, scarce runway and terminal slots at congested hubs such as London Heathrow (LHR) and Hong Kong (HKG) limit how often an airline can land or take off. Putting a 787 into a single Heathrow slot where a 517-seat A380 can operate leaves far fewer seats for sale at peak demand, not something that Emirates sees as acceptable.

    Emirates reinforces those slot economics through its connecting hub in Dubai, which pulls transfer passengers from across continents onto high-capacity long-haul flights. Whereas other major airports focus on point-to-point local demand at either end of a route, Dubai funnels connecting traffic into large cabins, so seat occupancy stays consistently high. Together, scarce slots at major destinations and steady transfer flows at Dubai give Emirates the passenger volume needed to make high seat counts pay off.

    It has been revealed that few other carriers share the exact combination of network scale, slot pressure, and hub geography that lets Emirates run the A380 so consistently. Reporting from Simple Flying highlights that Emirates built its entire long-haul model around funneling global connecting traffic through Dubai onto high-capacity trunk routes. Many other airlines rely more heavily on local point-to-point demand or spread flying across fragmented secondary markets, where filling 500 seats every day is much harder to do consistently.

    In a recent development, differences in hub structure and slot portfolios also explain why rival operators often reach different conclusions about the double-decker. While some airlines face tight runway caps at destinations, they may lack a central connecting hub with the same global reach or fleet concentration to keep large cabins full across seasons. When demand dips or seasonal swings hit, carrying hundreds of empty seats penalizes operating margins far more severely than operating smaller twin-aisle jets.

    Those structural contrasts help explain why several carriers have parked or retired A380 aircraft earlier than Emirates, and why others have not made the A380 the focal point of their fleet. Take Air France, for example: the airline retired all its A380 aircraft in 2020, primarily because it could not fillseats like Emirates can. Without Emirates' specific mix of connecting scale and high-volume trunk demand, replicating its A380 formula remains out of reach for most airlines.

    Recent findings suggest that the A380's commercial case at Emirates is backed by years of financial results, not just theoretical seat math. Before the pandemic, Emirates President Tim Clark told Simple Flying that roughly 85% of Emirates' profits came from the A380 because the double-decker stayed consistently full and drew strong demand across every cabin. High occupancy across first, business, and economy turned those large passenger counts into substantial earnings across long-haul trunk routes.

    It has been revealed that that profit contribution has carried into Emirates' modern record run even as fuel expenses and operating costs remain closely watched. As detailed by Aviation Week and Emirates' 2025–26 annual financial results, Clark recently pointed to the A380 as the most profitable asset in Emirates' fleet during its record financial year. Broad demand for premium and main cabins helped support those results.

    It has been revealed that end-of-year financial figures highlight the scale of that record performance across both the airline and the wider group. Emirates' 2025–26 financial disclosures show Emirates Group reported a record profit of AED 24.4 billion (approximately $6.6 billion) for 2025–26, while Emirates airline posted a record profit before tax of AED 22.8 billion (approximately $6.2 billion). Together, those numbers show how well-filled A380 cabins can underpin strong financial returns and provide hard proof that the A380 remains a financially viable aircraft for Emirates.

    Recent findings suggest that looking ahead, Emirates looks to keep its A380 fleet flying until roughly 2041, giving the double-decker a long runway in service even after production ended in 2021. Coverage from Simple Flying and Executive Traveller notes that Emirates has worked to keep the fleet flying for years to come while weighing what comes next at the top end of its widebody lineup. Extending A380 operations toward 2041 reflects how central high-capacity flying remains to the airline's long-term fleet proposal.

    Sources indicate that to keep that superjumbo presence going with modern efficiency, Emirates President Tim Clark has floated a modernized A380neo concept and signaled readiness to order at least 100 aircraft, according to reporting in Executive Traveller. Clark estimates a re-engined and updated A380neo could burn around nine tonnes (approximately 19,842 pounds) of fuel per hour, which would narrow the running-cost gap against newer twinjets. From Emirates' perspective, a 100-jet commitment means the A380 should ideally continue operating well beyond 2041, as long as Airbus can find a way to improve its economics.

    Airbus, however, has set a much higher bar before reviving the program, reportedly pointing to roughly 250 orders needed to make a restart commercially viable. That gap between a 100-aircraft minimum order and a 250-order threshold creates a clear standoff with no launched A380neo program on the board. Unless order volume or manufacturing economics shift dramatically, Emirates' initiative for 2041 rests on its existing fleet rather than a newly built A380neo.

    The A380's story at Emirates reveals why high hourly fuel burn does not automatically doom a large aircraft when operating conditions line up. Burning roughly 4,600 gallons (approximately 17,413 liters) of jet fuel per hour looks daunting on paper, but high passenger loads, lower per-seat fuel burn than twin-aisle alternatives on busy trunks, scarce slots at hubs, and steady connecting flows through Dubai allow Emirates to turn that capacity into strong financial returns.

    According to recent reports, the A380 is still more of a specialized tool, not something viable across the wider industry. Few airlines possess the hub geography, slot portfolio, and connecting traffic scale required to keep five hundred-plus seats consistently full across long-haul sectors year after year through seasonal peaks and troughs. For Emirates, however, high hourly fuel burn and high seating capacity are two sides of the same commercial equation as long as trunk demand and connecting flows stay strong.

    ICAO Hosts Air Transport Conference, Elects New Council Members

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (745 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Airlinegeeks

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Last week, ICAO headquarters in Montréal hosted the Seventh Worldwide Air Transport Conference, where member states and industry stakeholders gathered to set global policy priorities on aviation economic regulation, infrastructure financing, resilience, consumer protection, and sustainable growth.
    • In a recent development, over 1,500 delegates from 154 member states and organizations attended the week-long event 13 years after the Sixth Conference in 2013.
    • “Broad agreement was reached on the need for harmonized, risk-based, and proportionate economic regulation that facilitates the adoption of emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence, automation, sustainable aviation fuels, and advanced air mobility solutions,” ICAO stated in a press release during the conference.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Last week, ICAO headquarters in Montréal hosted the Seventh Worldwide Air Transport Conference, where member states and industry stakeholders gathered to set global policy priorities on aviation economic regulation, infrastructure financing, resilience, consumer protection, and sustainable growth.

    In a recent development, over 1,500 delegates from 154 member states and organizations attended the week-long event 13 years after the Sixth Conference in 2013. They discussed high-level topics in commercial aviation: modernizing economic and legal frameworks, investing in infrastructure and skilled workforces, and ensuring that innovation keeps pace with rapidly changing technologies and global demands.

    “Broad agreement was reached on the need for harmonized, risk-based, and proportionate economic regulation that facilitates the adoption of emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence, automation, sustainable aviation fuels, and advanced air mobility solutions,” ICAO stated in a press release during the conference.

    Industry observers note that participants agreed on the value of frameworks that support innovation and investment for economic development. They stressed this especially for smaller landlocked states, which depend heavily on air connectivity for growth.

    Recent findings suggest that the conference supported modernizing air navigation infrastructure in line with ICAO’s Global Air Navigation Plan. It also supported liberalizing air service agreements without making liberalization conditional on infrastructure development, since newly introduced air links fostered by more liberal agreements are seen as key to economic growth.

    Sources indicate that however, all initiatives should be flexible enough to address local circumstances and should not burden developing states. ICAO’s statement continued: “The conference also reaffirmed that international standards are key to building effective, market-enabling policies and avoiding fragmentation that could impede cross-border air services. Delegates pointed to ICAO’s Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA) as a successful example of this approach.”.

    Participants were asked to express their views on consumer protection legislation that has become an integral part of the legal framework for all air operators.

    Industry observers note that at the Sixth Worldwide Air Transport Conference in March 2013, ICAO was asked to develop core principles on consumer protection. The final document, adopted by the ICAO Council in 2015, contains provisions on:.

    The report for the Seventh Conference invites states to modernize their consumer protection frameworks, keeping them evidence-based, proportionate, accessible, and responsive to the changing realities of commercial air transport. It also claims legislation should establish clear responsibilities for carriers, intermediaries, and other providers regarding information, complaints, and disruption assistance.

    ICAO is expected to review its core principles while preserving national and regional flexibility. It is also expected to assess whether existing policies adequately cover online intermediaries and other overlooked situations.

    Many member states cautioned against the ICAO Air Passenger Handbook proposed by IATA, because producing and maintaining a single repository covering many different national laws would be too costly.

    The conference asked ICAO to “examine the need for harmonized, risk-based guidance on the use of AI in aviation, including common terminology and meaningful human oversight.”.

    In a recent development, the rapid development of AI and its unknown effects on aviation operations is a topic member states will need to monitor. ICAO will coordinate and facilitate international exchange, while states will oversee implementation to ensure that the technologies adopted are secure, interoperable, and consistent with cybersecurity and data-protection objectives.

    ICAO will handle AI within its existing structure, as the proposal to create an ad hoc unit was not supported.

    During the final two days of the conference, ICAO held an extraordinary session of its assembly to elect the four additional council members required by the entry into force of the 2013 protocol amending the Convention on International Civil Aviation. The council is the organization’s permanent governing body, accountable to the assembly and responsible for setting priorities and implementing its directions. Its membership increased from 36 to 40, and there are no permanent seats.

    According to recent reports, six candidates competed for the four newly introduced seats: Ethiopia, Indonesia, Kazakhstan, Oman, Thailand, and Turkey. In the vote on the final day, Kazakhstan and Thailand were not elected, and the other four states won seats.

    The council now comprises Angola, Argentina, Australia, Belize, Brazil, Canada, China, Colombia, Cuba, Denmark, Ecuador, Egypt, Equatorial Guinea, Ethiopia, France, Germany, India, Indonesia, Italy, Japan, Malaysia, Mali, Mexico, Morocco, Nigeria, Oman, Poland, Qatar, the Republic of Korea, Saudi Arabia, Singapore, South Africa, Spain, Switzerland, Turkey, Uganda, the United Arab Emirates, the United Kingdom, the U.S., and Uruguay.

    The next elections will take place at the General Assembly in September 2028.
