    Chase and Hyatt have a pretty straightforward co-brand card portfolio, as there’s one personal card and one business card. Specifically, I’m talking about the World of Hyatt Credit Card and the World of Hyatt Business Credit Card.

    In a recent development, in this post, I’d like to compare the two cards, and talk about which is better. First let’s cover the details of both products, and then I’ll share my take on which is worth applying for. This is an especially good time to pick them up, given the current welcome offers.

    Link: Learn more about the World of Hyatt Credit Card or World of Hyatt Business Credit Card.

    To start, let’s cover the details of Hyatt’s two co-branded credit cards. Below is a chart with the basics, and I’ll go into a bit more detail below.

    Recent findings suggest that the World of Hyatt Credit Card (learn more) is Hyatt’s personal credit card, with a $95 annual fee. Hyatt’s personal credit card offers a variety of perks, including the following:.

    In a recent development, the World of Hyatt Business Credit Card (learn more) is Hyatt’s business credit card, with a $199 annual fee. Hyatt’s business credit card offers many benefits, including the following:.

    If you’re considering applying for a Hyatt credit card and would be eligible for a business or personal card, which should you apply for?

    The first thing to understand is that the World of Hyatt Card and World of Hyatt Business Card aren’t mutually exclusive. You could apply for both cards, and also earn the welcome bonus on each. So in some ways, it’s worth assessing the value of the cards independently, since you don’t actually have to decide between them.

    If you ask me, the World of Hyatt Card is a slam dunk if you stay at Hyatts with any frequency. The card has a reasonable annual fee, and it’s worth holding onto even if you don’t spend a dime on it.

    The annual free night award alone more than justifies the annual fee, and the five nights toward elite status with no spending requirement is a great perk as well. On top of that, I think there’s merit to spending $15,000 on the card per year, to earn a second annual free night award, plus to earn an additional six elite nights toward status.

    Industry observers note that the math on the World of Hyatt Business Card isn’t quite as straightforward. The card has a different welcome bonus than on the personal card, so there’s merit to picking up the card for that. But beyond that, the main reason you’ll want to get this card is because it offers the best rate of return on spending in terms of earning elite nights.

    With the business card, you can earn one elite night for every $2,000 spent, while with the personal card, you can get one elite night for every $2,500 spent (though the increments for earning elite nights differ).

    According to recent reports, so my best consolidated advice would be that the World of Hyatt Card is more valuable and is easier to justify, and is the best for the first $15,000 in spending annually. Beyond that, though, the World of Hyatt Business Card is best for helping to earn Hyatt status, especially if you’re a significant spender. Furthermore, it can be worth picking up the card in part for the huge bonus.

    Hyatt has both a personal and business co-branded credit cards. The products are totally different, and there’s potentially merit to both. The World of Hyatt Card is much easier to justify — the card has a lower annual fee, offers an annual free night award, provides five nights toward status without a spending requirement, and more.

    That being said, you don’t have to decide between the two cards, and there’s also merit to getting the World of Hyatt Business Card. The card has a better welcome bonus, and has the potential to be more rewarding for spending.

    #169887. Latest Update: Maine senators at odds over credit for earmarks

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (938 w)

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rollcall ↗ Open Full Page

    Latest Update: Maine senators at odds over credit for earmarks

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (938 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that collins took sole responsibility for a larger share of Maine earmarks.
    • After a bruising reelection defeat, Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins, R-Maine, is ready to play hardball.
    • Eager to show how much she's delivered for her constituents, Collins took the lion's share of credit in her committee's fiscal 2027 spending bills for Maine earmarks — at the expense of her delegation colleague, independent Angus King, who caucuses with Democrats.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that collins took sole responsibility for a larger share of Maine earmarks. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    After a bruising reelection defeat, Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins, R-Maine, is ready to play hardball.

    Eager to show how much she's delivered for her constituents, Collins took the lion's share of credit in her committee's fiscal 2027 spending bills for Maine earmarks — at the expense of her delegation colleague, independent Angus King, who caucuses with Democrats.

    The amount of earmarks King secured fell dramatically compared to his previous year's total in Senate Appropriations Committee bills, as Collins took sole credit for most earmarks both senators had requested.

    The power play has instigated a dispute over how to award credit for "congressionally directed spending," better known as earmarks. It has also raised questions about a Senate rule that requires committee leaders to disclose the name of each senator who requested projects to be included in a spending bill before it can move on the floor.

    According to recent reports, it’s undeniable that as the chair of the spending panel, Collins has more influence over which projects reach the final bills than her delegation mate. Collins spokesperson Phoebe Keller mentioned that since available earmark funding is split into separate pots for the majority and minority to dole out, the bills reflect which of those funding sources was tapped to provide money to the relevant projects.

    Keller said that Collins deserves sole credit for the contested projects, as listed in the reports accompanying the bills.

    "When only Collins is listed, it reflects only she chose to fund the project,” Keller mentioned.

    A Democratic committee aide contested that characterization, saying that traditionally all requesters are named regardless of which party’s funding allocation is tapped for a project.

    “The handling of these particular projects is a clear departure from the norm and will need to be rectified in conference negotiations,” the aide stated.

    King is credited with approximately $54 million in fiscal 2027 earmarks in the bills Collins released this month, including joint projects with Collins. That's down from around $231 million in the Senate's fiscal 2026 bills, according to a CQ Roll Call analysis.

    Industry observers note that last year, King and Collins were both listed on 75 of the 77 projects that both requested that were included in the Senate bills, with just two carrying only Collins’ name. This year, Collins claimed sole responsibility for over $125 million in projects that both she and King requested, approximately two-thirds of the joint requests.

    While King’s overall requests fell by more than $200 million this year versus last, his success in securing requested funds plummeted at a far greater rate with less credit for overlapping projects.

    The joint requests for which Collins claimed sole credit include five for the Maine Department of Transportation in the Transportation-HUD bill, including $10.7 million for northern freight rail improvements; $9.6 million for Route 26 reconstruction in Oxford; and $7.2 million for improvements in Rockport, among others.

    In the Labor-HHS-Education bill, projects Collins took sole credit for include $4 million for the University of Maine for biology laboratory equipment and just over $4 million for the creation of a modern emergency helipad at Lincoln Hospital.

    And the Interior-Environment bill features $4 million each for wastewater improvements in Limestone and Kennebec that both Collins and King asked for but are only attributed to Collins, among others.

    Similarly, the Agriculture, Commerce-Justice-Science and Homeland Security bills all include a project requested by both senators that only Collins is listed as securing in the bill.

    The outgoing Appropriations chair’s ability to fuel billions of dollars in federal funding for her state during her career was the centerpiece of her ultimately unsuccessful campaign for reelection, which she lost to Democrat Troy Jackson.

    As written, the draft bills appear to risk running afoul of a Senate rule that requires the committee’s chair to identify each senator who requested projects in a bill online at least 48 hours before a vote to advance the legislation on the floor.

    The relevant rule, Senate Rule 44, states that it is out of order to vote on a motion to proceed to consider a bill unless the chairman of the committee certifies that “each congressionally directed spending item . . . has been identified through lists, charts, or other similar means including the name of each Senator who submitted a request to the committee for each item so identified.”.

    That information must be “available on a publicly accessible congressional website in a searchable format at least 48 hours before such vote.”.

    A King spokesman called on the spending panel to add his name to the relevant requests.

    “We believe this must have been an oversight and assume the committee will update the requests —per Senate rules — once it’s called to their attention,” King spokesman Matthew Felling mentioned.

    The bills released by Collins are drafts, and no floor action on final fiscal 2027 spending bills is expected this Congress. There’s limited time left before the Dec. 11 spending deadline, when all current funding is set to expire, and Democrats want to wait to negotiate final bills until they retake majorities in both chambers next year.

    But to comply with the rule, before the bills reach the floor the reports accompanying the bills, that includes the earmark tables, may have to be rewritten to list King on the contested projects, or the committee may need to disclose the information elsewhere online.

    Both chambers unveiled stricter ethics guidelines surrounding earmarks in 2021 when the practice returned after a decade-long ban.

    Peter Cohn contributed to this report.

    #169886. Royal Air Maroc Business Class Boeing 737 Review: Good For A Short Hop

    📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2190 w)

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Onemileatatime ↗ Open Full Page

    Royal Air Maroc Business Class Boeing 737 Review: Good For A Short Hop

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2190 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • To kick off the return portion of our Orient Express adventure via Africa trip, we flew Royal Air Maroc’s Boeing 737-800 business class on the 45-minute flight from Malaga (AGP) to Casablanca (CMN).
    • According to recent reports, I must admit, Royal Air Maroc has a really solid short haul product.
    • Admittedly the flight attendant serving us didn’t have much personality, and the cabin wasn’t in great condition.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    To kick off the return portion of our Orient Express adventure via Africa trip, we flew Royal Air Maroc’s Boeing 737-800 business class on the 45-minute flight from Malaga (AGP) to Casablanca (CMN).

    According to recent reports, I must admit, Royal Air Maroc has a really solid short haul product. While there’s no Wi-Fi or seat back entertainment, I appreciate that the airline has “proper” business class seats, the inflight meal service was outright generous for such a short flight, and I also appreciated the dedicated business class bus upon arrival.

    Admittedly the flight attendant serving us didn’t have much personality, and the cabin wasn’t in great condition. But still, those are hardly huge concerns. For that matter, it has to be acknowledged how the airlines of northern Africa really lower the bar when it comes to the quality of the inflight experience (hi, Air Algerie!), so on a relative basis, this was rather excellent.

    Recent findings suggest that ford and I booked an itinerary on Royal Air Maroc all the way from Malaga to Miami via Casablanca. The reason was because the airline offered the best schedule that would get us home the same day after our Orient Express Sailing Yachts cruise.

    Royal Air Maroc often makes only one business class seat available, so I had to get a bit creative to make this work. I ended up booking one ticket using 57,500 American AAdvantage miles plus $85.72 in taxes & fees, while the other ticket was booked with cash, at the cost of $1,620, with the following itinerary:.

    10/09 AT989 Malaga to Casablanca departing 2:15PM arriving 1:30PM10/09 AT204 Casablanca to Miami departing 3:00PM arriving 7:45PM.

    Obviously paying cash for a ticket wasn’t ideal, but that still ended up being less out of pocket than flying British Airways business class through London on awards, factoring in the carrier surcharges.

    In a recent development, we arrived at Malaga Airport at around 11:30AM, plenty early for our 2:15PM flight. We headed through security and then cleared passport control… only then did I realize that the non-Schengen lounge is currently closed, so we had no lounge option there.

    Recent findings suggest that I guess we could’ve exited passport control again to access the lounge in the Schengen area of the terminal, but we figured that wasn’t worth it, so we just decided to grab a seat. I have to say, the non-Schengen portion of the Malaga Airport had quite the scene. Virtually every other flight departing around the same time was on Jet2, and it was definitely a “festive” spirit in the terminal. Based on the passengers, you’d think the airport had banned close-toed shoes.

    Sources indicate that boarding for our flight was scheduled for 1:30PM, 45 minutes before departure, from gate B16. Sure enough, that’s exactly when boarding started, with business class passengers being invited to board first.

    In a recent development, we boarded the Royal Air Maroc Boeing 737-800 through the forward door, and then turned right into the business class cabin. Royal Air Maroc’s 737s have 12 business class seats, spread across three rows, in a 2-2 configuration.

    According to recent reports, royal Air Maroc’s 737 business class seats are particularly spacious, as they boast 43″ of pitch and 21″ of width, with 6″ of recline. So this is significantly more spacious than what you’d find in domestic first class within the United States, where pitch is more commonly around 37-38″ — an extra 5-6″ is definitely noticeable!

    These seats have little foot bars that fold down from the seat in front, for extra support while inflight. These were also old style seats, in terms of having large, deep, leather pockets on the seat back.

    The tray table folded out from the side of the seat, and had to be flipped over to be fully extended. It was a bit flimsy, as the cabin definitely felt a bit past its prime.

    There was a center console where drinks could be placed during the flight, along with additional little drink trays that could be extended, acting as “wings” to the center console.

    On the front side of the center console were the AC charging outlets, which were the extent of the charging options there — there were no USB-A or USB-C charging options.

    There were also little channel and volume controls, along with a headphone jack, for tuning into the inflight entertainment.

    Perhaps the most modern part of the cabin was the overhead consoles, which had the more modern Boeing overhead lights and air nozzles.

    Recent findings suggest that while the cabin definitely felt tired and wasn’t in great shape, the comfort was otherwise great, when compared to what you’ll otherwise find in the region. I mean, my previous two regional flights on airlines from northern Africa were on junky wet leased planes, so this was luxurious by comparison.

    Unfortunately this Royal Air Maroc 737 didn’t have any sort of Wi-Fi or streaming entertainment. Instead, there were monitors that folded down from the overhead consoles, which had some programming during the flight — on this flight, there were cartoons.

    So the entertainment situation was disappointing, but of course on a flight of this length, it wasn’t an issue. But if I were on a three or four hour flight on one of these 737s, I’d of course have a different impression.

    During boarding, the crew came around with pre-departure drinks, including the choice of water or lemon mint juice, and we got one of each. They were served in proper glassware — I love the branding!

    One thing I have to mention is that the cabin was insanely hot during boarding — I imagine the APU wasn’t working, or something, so we were sweating our you-know-whats off.

    Industry observers note that airlines of northern Africa are always a bit funny when it comes to safety. At 1:55PM the safety video was screened, while the door was still open, and before all passengers had boarded.

    According to recent reports, at 2:05PM the main cabin door closed, with seven of the 12 business class seats occupied. At 2:10PM we began our pushback, and at 2:15PM we began our taxi. There were zero security checks during the taxi out, and a couple of people in business class had their seats reclined.

    The captain sure was a good multi-tasker, or at least so I assume — he made his welcome aboard announcement while also taxiing us out and making some turns (at least I assume that at Royal Air Maroc taxiing is a captain-only function, but maybe that’s not the case?).

    It has been revealed that it was just a quick taxi out to runway 13, where we were second in line for takeoff, behind a Ryanair 737. We were cleared for takeoff at 2:20PM, with some nice views on the climb out.

    The seatbelt sign was turned off just five minutes after takeoff, at which point the crew sprung into action, starting by closing the curtain between the cabin and the galley.

    After takeoff, the crew distributed some warm towels, which had a nice scent to them.

    A few minutes later, the inflight meal was brought out. For a flight of this length, I was impressed. The main dish had some prawns, burrata, and veggies. Then there was a cheese plate, a slice of cake, and a piece of bread. Unlike on Air Algerie, a little thought was also put into presentation.

    The crew passed through with water, while other drinks had to specifically be requested. I asked for a cup of tea, which was also promptly served. By the time I finished my snack, we were already well into our descent.

    For a flight of this length, this kind of snack is really tough to beat.

    Just before landing, I checked out the business class lavatory on the Royal Air Maroc 737. It was a pretty standard previous generation 737 lavatory, and had definitely seen better days. Among other things, the toilet seat just wouldn’t stay up unless you held it open the entire time.

    There were no special amenities, other than Royal Air Maroc branded hand lotion.

    Recent findings suggest that the lead flight attendant on this flight was a nice older guy. We didn’t interact with him much, but he seemed generally charming. For example, I saw him kindly bring some toys to a kid seated in business class, and engage nicely with him.

    The primary flight attendant working in business class was a younger lady. She wasn’t rude, but had zero outward personality. She didn’t smile, and if we exchanged five words, that would’ve been a lot. But at least she was efficient and on top of things, and compared to Air Algerie, she was basically a Singapore Airlines flight attendant.

    Industry observers note that at 1:50PM Casablanca time (there was a one-hour time change from Malaga, so this was 30 minutes after takeoff), the seatbelt sign was turned on, as we were well into our descent to Casablanca. At that point the pre-landing announcement was made, but again, there was nothing in the way of safety checks, and the person seated in front of me even still had a glass at their seat.

    The views on the approach were lovely — Morocco really is a beautiful country.

    We ended up landing at Casablanca Airport at 1:05PM, on runway 35L.

    From there we had a short five-minute taxi to our arrival stand, where we’d have to get on a bus to get to the terminal.

    On the plus side, this gave us a great view of the 737 we had just flown, which was in the special oneworld livery.

    Recent findings suggest that as we deplaned, the lead flight attendant and captain kindly bid farewell to everyone. The airline did have a special bus for business class passengers, which is at least a nice aspect of the passenger experience, as it shows some effort.

    It was a roughly five-minute ride to the terminal, then we cleared security, and then we boarded our Royal Air Maroc 787 business class flight to Miami a short while later.

    I had a pleasant flight in Royal Air Maroc’s 737 business class. For a 45-minute flight, it sure is nice to get real business class seats and a proper, tasty snack. The flight also operated on schedule, so I really have no complaints, especially when you consider the typical airline experience in the northern part of Africa.

    To be fair, though, the cabin was definitely a bit tired, and the lack of Wi-Fi and streaming entertainment would prove more frustrating on a longer journey. Furthermore, the primary flight attendant working business class just didn’t have any personality.

    What do you make of Royal Air Maroc’s 737 business class?

    It has been revealed that I don't know why, but I really enjoyed this review. Thanks Ben! I've found a few RAM AAdvantage redemptions from time to time that I booked then had to cancel. So I have some FOMO on a connection in Casablanca...

    RAM is a notoriously bad airline that is very often criticised for appalling management, disgraceful client relations, disagreeable employees (probably because they're badly paid), systematic problems concerning lost luggage, old aircraft lacking modern facilities, questionable safety procedures...the list goes on and on. This "review" confirms many of these criticisms whilst giving it credit for services that are banal for any other, competent airline, and drawing the bizarre conclusion in writing that it's better "compared to other African airlines".     #169885. Air France Economy Class: Impressions From A Flight Across The Atlantic

    📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1804 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Onemileatatime ↗ Open Full Page

    Air France Economy Class: Impressions From A Flight Across The Atlantic

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1804 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In the spirit of trying out fresh ideas and topics here at OMAAT, and having learned that many of you are interested in reading about economy, here are some thoughts about how well Air France does the job.
    • It has been revealed that I’ll focus on the daytime return flight from Dublin (DUB) back to Rio (GIG) via Paris (CDG), as I slept through as much of the outbound overnight as I could.
    • After completing this trip, I’ve flown back and forth between Brazil and France in all four of Air France’s cabin classes.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In the spirit of trying out fresh ideas and topics here at OMAAT, and having learned that many of you are interested in reading about economy, here are some thoughts about how well Air France does the job.

    It has been revealed that I’ll focus on the daytime return flight from Dublin (DUB) back to Rio (GIG) via Paris (CDG), as I slept through as much of the outbound overnight as I could. This is not a full review — rather, it’s some general comments on the seats, food, and tech, in Air France’s economy offering.

    After completing this trip, I’ve flown back and forth between Brazil and France in all four of Air France’s cabin classes. Yes, including La Première – I do fly in the pointy end sometimes. 😉.

    Having transited through Paris Charles de Gaulle so many times now, I’m actually starting to learn my way around the crazy maze of terminals.

    Industry observers note that on this occasion, the transfer was on the simpler side, as both flights used gates in Terminal 2E. That said, I still had to catch the light rail transit from Hall K to Hall L and pass through a full security screening before entering the departures area. Not all airports in Europe require this, and I hope it’s taken into account when CDG simplifies its terminal numbering, which is expected in March 2027.

    Thanks to my Flying Blue Gold status, I had access to Air France’s Hall L Lounge, which is at the moment undergoing some refurbishments.

    Getting a post- or pre-flight facial would have been amazing, but, like my five previous visits to Air France’s lounges in Paris, I’ve had no luck at getting a slot.

    Either there were simply no slots left, or, as on this visit, the remaining slot(s) were after my departure time.

    Industry observers note that speaking of lounges, I took this photo from Air France’s lounge in Terminal 2E, Hall K, on a previous trip. According to a staffer I spoke with, the construction outside will eventually be a huge newly introduced flagship Air France lounge for Terminal 2E.

    I sent this photo to Ben before I boarded, and he was surprised to see that the board specifically referenced pre-boarding for Flying Blue Ultimate members. In case you didn’t know either, now you do.

    Here’s one final pic for the AvGeeks: even though Air France’s version of the A380 wasn’t particularly loved, the elevated jetbridge above the Boeing 777-300ER in this pic was a nostalgic reminder of the airline’s former superjumbos.

    If you’re locking in for 10+ hour flight in economy, there’s only a limited level of comfort that any airline would be able to offer. I wasn’t envious at all walking through the premium economy cabin during boarding….

    Thanks to my Flying Blue Gold status, I was able to choose any seat in the cabin from 72 hours before departure. Contrary to my avoidance of bulkhead/exit row seats and their fixed armrests on night flights, I picked bulkhead window seat 21L in the front row of the economy cabin.

    Sources indicate that the legroom here was more than I needed for this day flight. My plan was to spend most of the flight working, so this seat also avoided anyone reclining into my laptop.

    Of Air France’s three Airbus A350-900 configurations, this was the newest 292-seater version that has been rolling out since 2023. The economy cabin has 212 seats in a 3-3-3 layout, which I know isn’t usually a favorite of families of four. Non-bulkhead/exit row seats have a pitch of around 31 inches.

    I didn’t move the four-way adjustable headrest at all during the flight, and the recline is listed as being around 118 degrees.

    No matter where I’m sitting, I can’t help but marvel at that wingtip.

    It has been revealed that of the 29 flights I’ve taken with Air France, I can only remember one meal that wasn’t good. In fact, it was terrible, and was actually when I was flying premium economy from Paris to Zanzibar (ZNZ) in 2024.

    Of the two meal choices, I went for the chicken pasta (I didn’t note down the second option as I only decided to write about this after the flight).

    In a recent development, I thoroughly enjoyed the main dish. It had lots of protein, the sauce was flavorful, and the little mini pasta pieces weren’t dry at all. Given the several accompaniments, I consider this a generous helping of food. The Président camembert cheese was a nice premium touch, and the bread roll was quite the opposite of stale. I can’t tell you how good the mini apple tart was, as I’m intolerant to apples.

    In a recent development, I wish there had been a menu so I could know for sure what was in this really tasty salad. I’m pretty sure it was a mix of mainly carrots, potato, and barley, in what I guess was a honey mustard sauce.

    According to recent reports, for those who don’t know, Air France differentiates itself by serving Champagne in economy. Partial though I can be, I stuck to Coke Zero for the caffeine.

    I like the intention of using wood instead of plastic for cutlery; I just wish the knife could actually cut!

    Despite the hefty lunch serving, I got very hungry midway through the flight as I didn’t eat a proper breakfast. I went to raid the snack baskets at the rear-most galley. The area very busy with lots of passengers lingering, and there was some kerfuffle over a medical matter, so I didn’t take any pictures.

    Industry observers note that I did, however, get a snap of my snack haul. A mini ice cream, a couple of chocolate truffles, a packet of savory biscuits, and half a cheese sandwich. While the snacks might have lacked in nutrition, it’s nice to know that you won’t go hungry on Air France’s economy flights.

    Sources indicate that I was so tired after the 3:30 a.m. alarm that I skipped the pre-landing light meal on the return flight in favor of a nap.

    It has been revealed that neither did I touch the box containing a very beige selection of a bread roll and a pastry on the flight to Paris from Rio. Craving caffeine after a patchy night of sleep, I attempted the drip-style coffee, but a sip was enough to turn my nose up. Yes, I am a coffee snob, and I’m proud of it.

    Industry observers note that air France made a great choice to mount the IFE screens on the bulkhead. Only the screen in the aisle seat in my row of three was in that annoying underseat position that needs to be folded away for takeoff and landing.

    Recent findings suggest that I could just about reach the very tactile screen when leaning forward. Otherwise, there was a mousepad-style remote.

    The 13.3-inch screens are among the largest in the industry, and are the same size as those in the premium economy cabin on this plane.

    I counted four charging outlets: a USB-C and a USB-A port in the IFE screen, and, under the seat, a regular power outlet and a second USB-C port.

    Recent findings suggest that as for Wi-Fi connectivity, there were no disruptions to the complimentary Starlink for the duration of the flight. However, the whole IFE system had to be reset shortly after we took off. Then, a few hours into the flight, the vast majority of the movies disappeared from the system, including the one I was halfway through. I was able to connect my AirPods to the screen with no problem.

    Other amenities, so to speak, were a rather coarse pillow, a blanket, and over-the-head headphones.

    One of my favorite things about flying and traveling is meeting new people, including cabin crew, though due to the busyness of economy cabins, that can be tough.

    According to recent reports, if I have time, I also try to bring a sweet treat on board for the crew to enjoy during the flight, no matter which cabin I’m flying in, as it is usually a great way to build rapport. It worked on this flight, as several crew members came to thank me for the mince pies. Mattieu, to whom I handed them during boarding, brought me a little note to say thanks for both the pies and my Flying Blue loyalty.

    Over the course of the flight, I noticed crew in the economy cabin engaging enthusiastically with passengers. At the start of interactions during meal service, I even heard crew asking passengers whether their preferred language was English or French. On at least three occasions, I noticed crew walking through the cabin offering water.

    According to recent reports, after being spoiled with lots of lie-flat beds over the years, I’ll admit the pre-flight excitement isn’t quite the same when boarding a long-haul flight in economy. This return trip in Air France economy was perfectly fine, with the pros certainly outweighing the cons.

    Whether you only fly business class, or a frequent economy class flier, I hope you gained some insights into the Air France economy experience.

    • It has been revealed that I’m thankful for my older son’s soccer coach, who has known him for over three years now, moving my boy up from an in-house program, to a Sunday league, and this fall to the EDP (Elite Development Program), where this cheap-as-chips town team plays (and usually defeats) all the expensive “academy teams” in our area.
    • Michael Brendan Dougherty is a senior writer at National Review Online.

    In a recent development, I’m thankful for one little moment on Monday this week, around 5:05 p.m. The dark of night was falling over most of the sky, except for a brilliant ring of purple just over the tree line to one side of us. We pulled the minivan into the parking lot of the karate studio, and my eight-year-old son hopped out of the car, grabbing my hand as we passed through the parking lot. I gave it a little squeeze, and he squeezed it back. Maybe just a few more years of that. He earned his first stripes on his white belt that night.

    It has been revealed that I’m thankful for my older son’s soccer coach, who has known him for over three years now, moving my boy up from an in-house program, to a Sunday league, and this fall to the EDP (Elite Development Program), where this cheap-as-chips town team plays (and usually defeats) all the expensive “academy teams” in our area. My son was not, at first, a natural athlete — in fact, he was quite clumsy. But he had this enormous engine in him to run, and over the years developed patience for himself to work. His coach recognized him, coached his oversensitivity out of him, made him work — and enjoy working — harder than he ever would have done just by himself.

    Michael Brendan Dougherty is a senior writer at National Review Online.

    Recent findings suggest that there’s no denying that traveling by air can be stressful, and that it’s extremely frustrating when things go wrong. Furthermore, not everyone is a frequent traveler, and understands the ins and outs of how the airline industry functions.

    Recent findings suggest that so that brings us to a complaint from last night from an American Airlines passenger. The complaint is so incredibly off base in the first place. But what’s even worse is that when this person is confronted with reality, he just doubles down and keeps going. This person deserves to be roasted, and if you ask me, should be banned from the airline.

    Late last night, a social media user posted a picture of two airline pilots on X, with the following caption:.

    I won’t be seeing my family this Thanksgiving because a couple pilots couldn’t drink a cup of coffee and get us home. They clocked out in two hours, but we had 3 hr flight. Thanks @AmericanAir.

    In a recent development, I won't be seeing my family this Thanksgiving because a couple pilots couldn't drink a cup of coffee and get us home. They clocked out in two hours, but we had 3 hr flight. Thanks @AmericanAir pic.twitter.com/q1I8pjsM3w.

The airline industry operates with the goal of putting safety above all else, and pilot fatigue has been a contributing factor to many accidents over the years.

    I totally get it, you want to be home for Thanksgiving, and it sucks things went wrong, but those are the facts. This is federal law, and on top of that, we should want pilots to be well rested, rather than just saying “keep working, just have another cup of coffee.”.

    #169880. Tech Report: House Democrats eye stock trading ban as early priority next Congress

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1317 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rollcall ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: House Democrats eye stock trading ban as early priority next Congress

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1317 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, here at a news conference on Capitol Hill last week, indicates banning stock trading in Congress is a “high priority.” Now Democrats must decide what form their push will take.
    • After stock trading became a major talking point on the campaign trail this fall, Democrats are feeling pressure to push through a bill in the new year.
    • But banning trading by members of Congress may not be easy, and some worry the issue could get bogged down in larger debates over the party’s anti-corruption agenda.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, here at a news conference on Capitol Hill last week, indicates banning stock trading in Congress is a “high priority.” Now Democrats must decide what form their push will take. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    After stock trading became a major talking point on the campaign trail this fall, Democrats are feeling pressure to push through a bill in the new year.

    But banning trading by members of Congress may not be easy, and some worry the issue could get bogged down in larger debates over the party’s anti-corruption agenda.

    Sources indicate that “I’d rather have it be a clean bill focused on stock trading, and not muddy it by adding other topics, even if they’re good policies,” stated Rep. Seth Magaziner, D-R.I.

    According to recent reports, the incoming majority could plant a flag on government accountability with a broad package ranging from insider trading to campaign finance and more. Or they could zoom in on the stocks matter with a standalone bill.

    Magaziner noted he hasn’t received any assurances from House Democratic leaders, instead describing a “collaborative conversation” about what form the legislation could take.

    “I worry that it would get weighed down under its own weight if you try to load it up with too many things,” Magaziner said, while stressing he would support whatever expected incoming Speaker Hakeem Jeffries decides.

    Meanwhile, more than half of the Democrats in the incoming freshman class are calling for action on Day One of the new Congress, sending a letter to Jeffries last week suggesting they make a “down payment on much-needed reform” by changing House rules to curb stock trading.

    “Democrats may have won the election, but we have a long way to go to earn back the trust of voters across the country,” reads the letter, led by Reps.-elect Sarah Trone Garriott of Iowa and Jamie Ager of North Carolina. “A stock trading ban alone will not fix Washington, but it is the fastest way to show voters we heard them.”.

    Folding new language into the House’s internal rules would be a relatively easy path, requiring just a majority vote on the House floor, instead of passage in both chambers and the president’s signature. But such internal limits wouldn’t have the force of law, and some believe it would cool the urgency around the problem while doing little to crack down on insider trading.

    According to recent reports, colorado Rep. Jason Crow noted moving forward promptly with a rule change wouldn’t preclude passing a bill, suggesting his fellow Democrats do both.

    “I want to pursue a parallel track,” remarked Crow, who co-chairs the End Corruption Caucus. “We want to move via rule and just prohibit it right out of the gate, or as much as we can.”.

    Jeffries has repeatedly noted the topic is high on his to-do list as he looks to deliver on the accountability the “American people are demanding.”.

    Sources indicate that “We’re committed to making sure we pass legislation that bans members of Congress from trading stocks. That will be a high priority,” he remarked at a news conference this week.

    But with more than two dozen different bills on the topic introduced over the past few years alone, lawmakers will have to decide exactly what a “ban” means to them.

    Some want to force members of Congress to fully offload their stocks with the exception of widely held mutual funds. Other proposals would block lawmakers from buying fresh stocks but allow them to keep the ones they already own, like a Republican-led bill that passed the House earlier this year but stalled in the Senate.

    Democrats resisted that push, which was led by outgoing House Administration Chair Bryan Steil, R-Wis., partly because it included an unrelated voter ID provision they called a “poison pill.” Many also complained the measure didn’t go far enough, extending to members’ spouses and dependent children but leaving out key figures in other branches of government, such as the president.

    It has been revealed that rep. Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash., noted she wants to stay close to the text of a consensus bill she hammered out last year with a small bipartisan group that included Magaziner and Reps. Chip Roy, R-Texas, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., Tim Burchett, R-Tenn., and Brian Fitzpatrick, R-Pa.

    “That is the most comprehensive, thorough, thoughtful proposal and bipartisan proposal that we have,” she stated of the bill, dubbed the Restore Trust in Congress Act.

    Recent findings suggest that that measure would not apply to President Donald Trump, as many Democrats have urged as they seek to draw attention to his ballooning wealth while in office. Still, Jayapal suggested a presidential stock trading ban could be moved separately.

    “There is discussion about the president, vice president, Cabinet, Supreme Court. I know we’re working on some language around enforcement, around those pieces, but I actually think that can be a separate bill,” Jayapal mentioned. “We want to hold everyone accountable — but at minimum, we have to do ourselves.”.

    Recent findings suggest that it’s not clear how much appetite will exist next year for a bipartisan compromise that could realistically clear a 60-vote cloture threshold in the Senate. Notably, key Republicans who worked on the consensus bill will be leaving Congress, with Roy losing a primary bid for Texas attorney general and Fitzpatrick unseated by a Democratic challenger.

    While lawmakers could in theory advance a newly introduced stock-trading bill even sooner, before Democrats take control of both chambers, time and patience is short in the lame-duck session.

    At a news conference at the Capitol earlier this week with Crow and Jayapal, a group of freshman and returning Democrats took matters into their own hands, promising not to hold or trade individual stocks as part of a broader pledge backed by the Political Integrity Project.

    Industry observers note that “My district, Latest York 10, happens to include Wall Street, but I don’t represent Wall Street. I represent the people of Brooklyn and Manhattan who deserve someone who goes to work every single day and indicates right up front, ‘I work for you.’ And what better way to prove that than by day one showing we will ban members of Congress from enriching themselves, from trading stocks?” Rep.-elect Brad Lander said.

    While momentum has grown in recent years as key senior lawmakers softened their resistance to a stock trading bill, not everyone is on board. Some members still argue, whether publicly or privately, that they should be able to trade on the stock market just like other citizens or that existing disclosure requirements established by a 2012 law are already enough to discourage dubious trades.

    As they iron out the legislative text of any new bill, members will have to decide how to handle emerging topics such as prediction markets and crypto, along with sticky questions such as whether to allow blind trusts. And extending restrictions to the president could be a nonstarter for many Republicans.

    Industry observers note that sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., said Democrats in the next Congress should look to a bipartisan bill that advanced out of the Senate Homeland and Governmental Affairs Committee in July 2025 as a model.

    “The legislation we passed out of the committee applied to the executive branch,” he said. “But it didn’t take effect for anybody until their next terms, which was a compromise.”.

    That proposal would apply to future presidents but not the current one, potentially freeing up more Republicans to vote for it without angering Trump. Still, it hasn’t seen action on the Senate floor.

    Hawley noted that while he’d like to see a “full ban on trading and holding” in Congress, he would be open to a weaker proposal in the interest of getting something done.

    “I’ll take anything that’s an incremental improvement over what we have now, which is nothing,” he said.

    Aris Folley contributed to this report.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that kimpton has a pretty cool “social password” concept, whereby you can receive extra perks for sharing a phrase at check-in. Kimpton generally has this promotion a couple of times per year — we last saw this in summer, and there’s now a new password for winter.

    I’d like to talk about what the latest password is, share my experience using it, and also pose a question to Kimpton regulars about the least cringeworthy way to go about saying it.

    Kimpton is one of the cooler IHG hotel groups, and there are a variety of things that set Kimpton apart from other IHG brands. One of those things is the social password. The idea is that seasonally, Kimpton provides a phrase through social media that you’re supposed to say when you check-in, and if you do that, you’ll receive something extra.

    Recent findings suggest that the new Kimpton password is “this calls for something,” and it’s valid for stays between November 27, 2026, and February 28, 2027. So just say that when you check-in at a Kimpton property during the promotion period, and you’ll receive a surprise.

    For those curious about what happens when you say the Kimpton password, I stayed at the Kimpton EPIC Miami some time back, which was my first Kimpton stay in quite a while (and I haven’t stayed at one since either). It was a good value as well, as I was able to use a free night award earned with the New IHG One Rewards Premier Credit Card (learn more).

    In a recent development, I was curious what the benefit would be for using the password. So I shared the password with the front desk agent. At the conclusion of the check-in experience, he brought out a game show-style wheel. I might have spun too hard, as it must have gone around for about 30 seconds. Go figure I landed on the tile that just had me spin again.

    It has been revealed that then I spun again, and the prize was free parking. I had a car and was staying for two nights, and parking costs $44 per night. So using the Kimpton password saved me nearly $100 — score!!

    Based on looking at the wheel, it seems that some of the other prizes include a free welcome drink, free breakfast, free snacks, and a free movie. There were also a few empty squares, where I guess you don’t win anything. And I’m not sure what the alarm clock, car tipping over, or postcard of Miami get you. Regardless, I’d say those are some awesome prizes, and I got a great reward.

    Sources indicate that it’s cute how the Kimpton EPIC Miami makes a game of this. I know there’s a lot of inconsistency when it comes to this benefit across Kimpton properties. Some hotels provide meaningful perks (an upgrade, free, parking, etc.), like I got here, while other hotels provide a 19 cent branded koozie.

    It’s great that this has stuck around, given that it has presumably become increasingly popular. Years ago not everyone was on social media, so it was a good way to encourage people to follow Kimpton on X, Facebook, Instagram, etc. With the way the internet has evolved, times have changed a bit.

    I’m sure I’m not the only one who finds the concept of saying a password at check-in to be kind of weird. So I think it’s fun to compare notes about how people share the password at the front desk. I find it awkward to just blurt out the password out of nowhere.

    So when I used this for my stay, I stated “I guess I’m supposed to say [social password] as the social password?” That did the trick, but I’d be curious to hear how other Kimpton regulars go about this!

    According to recent reports, between November 27, 2026, and February 28, 2027, Kimpton’s social password is “this calls for something.” Just state that phrase when you check-in at a Kimpton, and you should get some sort of a surprise. The gift will vary by property, so there’s no reason not to take advantage of this if staying at a Kimpton.

    enSights brings AI-powered business management to solar and storage operations

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (522 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Solarpowerworldonline

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that as solar and energy storage portfolios grow in both size and complexity, managing performance is just one part of the equation.
    • enSights is looking to bring those responsibilities together with the launch of its AI Studio, a new addition to its Energy Business Management (EBM) platform.
    • Recent findings suggest that the AI Studio is designed to give solar and storage owners, operators, and asset managers access to a customizable team of AI specialists that can support business and operational workflows.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that as solar and energy storage portfolios grow in both size and complexity, managing performance is just one part of the equation. Owners and operators must also keep track of power purchase agreements (PPAs), warranties, service contracts, billing, compliance requirements and project-level profitability.

    enSights is looking to bring those responsibilities together with the launch of its AI Studio, a new addition to its Energy Business Management (EBM) platform. The tech giant announced the launch Nov. 10.

    Recent findings suggest that the AI Studio is designed to give solar and storage owners, operators, and asset managers access to a customizable team of AI specialists that can support business and operational workflows. Through no-code tools, users can create AI dashboards and reports using natural-language instructions, while still establishing their own workflows, routines, data-access permissions and approval requirements.

    The approach here reflects a broader shift toward renewable energy software, it’s moving beyond monitoring individual assets toward managing the financial and operational performance of entire portfolios.

    Sources indicate that according to enSights, its EBM platform brings together energy management systems (EMS), production data, billing, PPA information, operations and maintenance, contractual obligations and compliance on a unified data foundation. That integration is central to the company’s AI strategy.

    Rather than limiting AI applications to identifying equipment issues or answering generation-related questions, the platform is designed to connect energy production with the contracts and financial obligations associated with each project.

    The AI Studio includes an orchestrator that coordinates specialized AI agents focused on areas like monitoring, operations, revenue, warranties, permits, lenders, insurers, and asset management. For portfolio managers, those capabilities could help reduce the time spent reviewing disconnected systems and manually reconciling information across departments. Automated reviews of contractual obligations, revenue performance and operational alerts could also help teams identify problems earlier and direct attention to matters that still require human intervention.

    The enSights AI Studio dashboard provides solar and energy storage operators with AI-powered tools for asset management, operational workflows, and financial oversight. Credit: enSights.

    enSights emphasized that people remain in control of the AI Team. Owners determine which workflows the agents handle and where approvals are required. Physical asset controls remain governed by established EMS and site-level systems.

    According to recent reports, the AI Studio also builds on an expanded financial management offering within the EBM platform. Its Financial Asset Management Module includes revenue assurance, contract, and obligation management, and profit-and-loss reporting.

    The module is intended to provide project-level financial visibility, helping companies identify and prevent revenue losses while generating reports for investors.

    The platform also includes real-time EMS, weather and tariff forecasting, along with dispatch planning intended to optimize revenue while maintaining grid safety and local compliance.

    Industry observers note that enSights states its platform is deployed globally across more than 100,000 sites, representing over 5 GW of assets. The company intends to demonstrate the AI Studio and its broader EBM platform at RE+ 2026.

    As AI gains traction across the clean energy industry, the next competitive advantage could come from connecting operational intelligence with the financial and contractual decisions that determine how successfully renewable energy portfolios perform.

    Citi AAdvantage Executive Card Review: Is The Admirals Club Perk Worth It?

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 21 min read (4152 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~21 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The Citi® / AAdvantage® Executive World Legend Mastercard® (formerly known as the Citi AAdvantage Executive World Elite Mastercard) is American Airlines’ most premium co-branded credit card, as part of the Citi partnership.
    • If you ask me, it’s one of the best value premium airline credit cards out there, and it’s also the airline credit card with the strongest lounge access perks.
    • According to recent reports, in this post, I’d like to take an in-depth look at the Citi AA Executive Card, with my Citi AAdvantage Executive Card review.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The Citi® / AAdvantage® Executive World Legend Mastercard® (formerly known as the Citi AAdvantage Executive World Elite Mastercard) is American Airlines’ most premium co-branded credit card, as part of the Citi partnership. While the Citi AA Executive Card has a steep annual fee, it offers strong perks, ranging from an Admirals Club membership, to the ability to supercharge your AAdvantage elite status, to credits that can help offset the annual fee.

    If you ask me, it’s one of the best value premium airline credit cards out there, and it’s also the airline credit card with the strongest lounge access perks. While products like the American Express Platinum Card® (learn more) and Chase Sapphire Reserve® Card (learn more) might typically be the first that come to mind when people consider premium cards, this one could make a lot more sense if you’re a frequent American flyer.

    According to recent reports, in this post, I’d like to take an in-depth look at the Citi AA Executive Card, with my Citi AAdvantage Executive Card review. I think this is especially important in light of the card’s recent refresh, where we saw the annual fee increase, but also saw new perks added.

    Link: Learn more about the Citi® / AAdvantage® Executive World Legend Mastercard®.

    Let me start by briefly summarizing the key details of the Citi AAdvantage Executive Card:.

    It has been revealed that this is the ideal card if you value American Admirals Club lounge access, if you’re going for elite status with American AAdvantage, or if you can just make the credits on the card work. If you’re just an occasional American flyer, there are probably more affordable options that will be easier to justify in the long term. However, with the card’s substantial welcome bonus, there’s a huge incentive to give this card a try.

    Sources indicate that one of the reasons that you’ll want to consider applying for the Citi AAdvantage Executive Card is because of the excellent welcome bonus it has. Of course that has to be balanced with the annual fee, and you also have to take into account the eligibility requirements, so let’s go through those details for the Citi AA Executive Card.

    The Citi AAdvantage Executive Card currently has a welcome bonus of 80,000 AAdvantage bonus miles after spending $8,000 within the first three months.

    It has been revealed that personally, I value American AAdvantage miles at ~1.5 cents each, so to me, those miles are worth about $1,200. That’s an excellent bonus, especially for a card that also offers a lot of value in the long run. There are so many great uses of AAdvantage miles, including for travel on partner airlines.

    For what it’s worth, I value Delta SkyMiles at 1.1 cents each, and United MileagePlus miles at 1.3 cents each, so these are the most valuable miles among the “big three” carriers, based on my math.

    The Citi AAdvantage Executive Card bonus miles aren’t available to those who have received a new cardmember bonus for this card in the past 48 months (however, you are eligible if you’ve had a different American Airlines credit card, including if you’ve received a bonus on a different product).

    Then there are the typical rules for Citi credit card applications, including that you can apply for at most one card with Citi every eight days, and at most two cards every 65 days.

    There’s not a consistent credit score that you need to get approved for the card, though I’d hope to have a score in the “good” to “excellent” range, ideally 700+ points. However, people with lower scores have been approved, and people with higher scores have been rejected, as it’s one of only many factors that determines eligibility.

    The Citi AAdvantage Executive Card has a $695 annual fee. There’s also a lot of value to adding authorized owners (as I’ll discuss below). You can expect to pay a total of $175 for up to three authorized users (so potentially under $60 each), and then each authorized user after that costs $175.

    Keep in mind that if you’re a Citigold customer, you can receive a $145 annual rebate on your annual fee, which is a nice perk.

    When it comes to spending money on the Citi AAdvantage Executive Card, here’s the rewards structure:.

    In terms of the reward for spending, there are potentially better cards for purchasing airline tickets, and also better cards for everyday spending. However, keep in mind that the most compelling reason to spend money on the card is in order to earn elite status with American Airlines. American Airlines uses its Loyalty Points system for status qualification, and credit card spending can help you earn status.

    American’s elite requirements are right now as follows, and you earn one Loyalty Point for every dollar spent on an American Airlines credit card:.

    Spending on the Citi AAdvantage Executive Card could earn you elite status, which I know will interest many. That’s the primary reason you’ll want to consider this card for spending.

    In a recent development, I do want to specifically point out one thing that throws people off — you earn one Loyalty Point per dollar spent on the card, unrelated to how many miles you earn for spending. In other words, if you’re making an American Airlines purchase, you’d earn 4x AAdvantage redeemable miles, but only 1x Loyalty Points on the purchase as such.

    In addition to earning one Loyalty Point for every dollar spent on the Citi AAdvantage Executive Card, you can also earn up to 40,000 Loyalty Points every year just for being a cardmember:.

    In other words, if you have this card, you’d only otherwise need to earn 170,000 Loyalty Points for Executive Platinum status, since this card would get you a boost of 30,000 Loyalty Points at that level. Those Loyalty Points can be earned in a variety of ways, ranging from flying, to online shopping, to credit card spending, to booking vacation packages. Either way, this Loyalty Points boost would be quite the advantage in terms of qualifying for Loyalty Point Rewards, and even upgrade priority.

    Sources indicate that the AAdvantage elite qualifying year goes from the beginning of March until the end of February of the following year. You don’t need to have the card at the beginning of the year to take advantage of this, so even if you open the card during the membership year, you could still earn 40,000 bonus Loyalty Points for that year (in other words, the credits can be retroactive).

    The Citi AAdvantage Executive Card has no foreign transaction fees, so this can be a good option for purchases abroad.

    While you’ll want to consult the full cardmember agreement and guide to benefits, the Citi AAdvantage Executive Card offers useful travel protection, including trip cancellation coverage, trip interruption coverage, trip delay protection, lost baggage protection, rental car coverage, and more.

    So this is a good card to potentially use for travel purchases, since you have to put them on your card to take advantage of those benefits.

    One of the main reasons you may want to get the Citi AAdvantage Executive Card is because of the lounge access perks that the card offers. Having the Citi AA Executive Card is the best way to access Admirals Clubs. Let’s discuss how that works.

    Sources indicate that the primary cardmember on the Citi AAdvantage Executive Card receives a full Admirals Club membership, including guesting privileges. That in and of itself is a reason this card makes sense.

    Industry observers note that while Admirals Clubs aren’t anything to get too excited about, they are improving nicely, in terms of design, and also in terms of the quality of food and beverages. I also appreciate the expansion of the Provisions by Admirals Club concept, whereby the airline offers Admirals Club members grab & go facility, where they can get some drinks or snacks to go before their flight.

    Ordinarily, if you were to buy a comparable Admirals Club membership with guesting privileges, you’d pay a minimum of $1,200 per year.

    By getting an Admirals Club membership with the Citi AAdvantage Executive Card, you’re saving $505-705 right off the bat.

    Note that while you can redeem miles for an Admirals Club membership, it’s a terrible value, as you’re getting only a cent per mile.

    What you get with the Citi AAdvantage Executive Card is a full Admirals Club membership, so you don’t even have to bring your credit card, as your membership will be linked to your AAdvantage number:.

    Admirals Club members don’t get access to Flagship Lounges, as that access is determined based on the ticket you purchased rather than any membership.

    In a recent development, many people may be considering applying for the Citi AAdvantage Executive Card shortly before taking an American Airlines trip. How soon after being approved for the card does your Admirals Club membership kick in?

    Recent findings suggest that since the primary cardmember gets a full Admirals Club membership, it’s linked to their AAdvantage account. Many may be surprised to learn that this membership could very well kick in before you even receive your credit card in the mail, and you don’t even need your card to enter a lounge.

    Industry observers note that fortunately, there’s an easy way to tell if your Admirals Club membership has been activated. To figure it out, pretend that you’re signing up for an Admirals Club membership. Go to this page, enter your AAdvantage number, last name, and password.

    If your account has already been updated to reflect the Admirals Club membership, you’ll see that the next page shows “1-Year Citi AADV Exec CC Membership.”.

    If it hasn’t been updated, you’ll see that it gives you the option of choosing what kind of membership you want to purchase.

    In a recent development, note that this only works for the primary cardmember. Since the authorized users don’t get a full Admirals Club membership, they wouldn’t show up as being eligible online. Authorized users need to present the physical Citi AAdvantage Executive Card, since there’s no membership linked to their AAdvantage account.

    The Citi AAdvantage Executive Card also offers Admirals Club access for authorized owners. As I explained above, you can add up to three authorized users for a total of $175, which potentially comes out to under $60 per authorized user. I’d say that’s a real sweet spot, since securing lounge access for friends and family for under $60 each is an amazing value.

    Note that authorized users receive Admirals Club access and not a membership, so there are the restrictions:.

    For the purposes of accessing Admirals Clubs this is more or less the same as an outright membership.

    On the next page, you’ll be able to manage authorized owners, including adding and removing them.

    You’ll just need their name to add them, and you have the choice of whether or not you want to give them permission to access your online account.

    Make sure you trust all your authorized users, since any charges they incur will be your responsibility.

    The primary reason to get the Citi AAdvantage Executive Card is because of the great welcome bonus, ability to earn status with spending, ability to receive 40,000 Loyalty Points annually just for being a cardmember, and Admirals Club benefit.

    According to recent reports, however, the Citi AA Executive Card offers some other perks that could add a lot of value for card members. These perks range from priority check-in at business class counters, to early boarding, to inflight or Admirals Club credits, to savings with American Airlines Vacations, Lyft, Avis, Budget, Global Entry, or TSA PreCheck, to elite status with Avis and Omni.

    Below is what you need to know about all the other perks of the Citi AAdvantage Executive Card.

    Recent findings suggest that those with the Citi AAdvantage Executive Card receive a first checked bag free on domestic American Airlines itineraries not just for themselves, but also for up to eight companions traveling on the same reservation. There’s no need to actually pay for the ticket with your Citi AAdvantage Executive Card — you just have to make sure it’s linked to your AAdvantage account (this benefit applies for the primary cardmember only).

    American ordinarily charges $45-50 for the first checked bag, so that’s a $90-100 value per person roundtrip (and if you had eight companions all checking a bag, that would be a value of $810-900).

    It has been revealed that one thing that sometimes throws off cardmembers is that this benefit doesn’t work for international flights, and it doesn’t work for a second bag, if your fare includes one bag. So just understand this is exclusively a first checked bag benefit on domestic flights.

    Sources indicate that for being the primary cardmember on the Citi AAdvantage Executive Card you receive several valuable airport benefits, including priority check-in, priority airport screening, and early boarding. These are all features that can save you time and money.

    There’s no need to show your card, as these perks should automatically be reflected with your ticket when you have your credit card linked to your AAdvantage account (which is automatic when you’re the primary cardmember).

    Industry observers note that the Citi AAdvantage Executive Card offers up to $500 in statement credits per calendar year toward American Airlines Vacations purchases. American Airlines Vacations is the carrier’s vacation package portal. This credit is semi-annual, meaning you can take advantage of a $250 credit every six months (once in January through June, and once in July through December).

    It has been revealed that this applies for a booking of two or more travel components, like a flight, car reservation, or hotel booking. Many people find American Airlines Vacations to be a great deal, and a good way to earn bonus Loyalty Points.

    The Citi AAdvantage Executive Card offers up to $200 in InKind credits every year. This comes in the form of a $100 semi-annual credit, with one being available January 1 through June 30, and the other being available July 1 through December 31. This can be used across multiple meals, and tips aren’t covered by the credit. Either the primary cardmember or authorized owners can use the perk, though authorized users don’t get extra credits.

    InKind is my favorite dining rewards app, and to me, this is basically good as cash. I dine at InKind restaurants constantly, as there are some really high quality restaurants on the list, so I value this new card perk immensely. If you’re new to InKind, make sure you also register through a refer-a-friend link, so you can get an extra credit.

    The Citi AAdvantage Executive Card offers up to $180 in Lyft credits every year. This comes in the form of a $15 Lyft credit each month after taking three eligible rides. The Lyft credit expires 30 days after it’s issued. Either the primary cardmember or authorized users can use the perk, though authorized users don’t get extra credits. Admittedly this requires quite a bit of effort to use, so not everyone will get value from that.

    Recent findings suggest that just for having the Citi AAdvantage Executive Card, you can receive up to $120 back on eligible Avis or Budget rentals every calendar year. Just charge an eligible pre-paid rental to your card each year, and you’ll receive a statement credit up to the $120 limit. This can be used toward a single rental or multiple rentals made directly with Avis or Budget. If you rent with Avis and Budget with any frequency, this could be worth face value.

    Sources indicate that just for having the Citi AAdvantage Executive Card, you can receive up to $100 in statement credits every calendar year toward spending onboard American flights, or in Admirals Clubs. So you can use this credit to purchase everything from premium drinks or snacks on flights, to premium alcoholic drinks in Admirals Clubs.

    Just charge the eligible purchase to your card, and you’ll be reimbursed automatically, with no registration required.

    Sources indicate that the Citi AAdvantage Executive Card offers a Global Entry or TSA PreCheck credit once every four years, which is worth up to $120. Simply charge the purchase to your card and it will automatically be reimbursed. You don’t have to be the one signing up — you can always pay for a friend or family member who is signing up instead.

    Personally, I always recommend applying for Global Entry, because Global Entry automatically comes with TSA PreCheck, while the inverse isn’t true.

    • Sources indicate that michael Brendan Dougherty has written a piece (“Even Putin Is a ’90s Nostalgist”) that I mostly agree with as far as it goes.
    • According to recent reports, I agree of course that Vladimir Putin would like the geographical disposition of NATO as it existed in 1997 but very much not its order of battle.
    • Daniel Foster is a contributing editor at National Review.

    Sources indicate that michael Brendan Dougherty has written a piece (“Even Putin Is a ’90s Nostalgist”) that I mostly agree with as far as it goes. My disagreement is largely confined to a few of its asides that nevertheless carry considerable weight for its underlying argument: that NATO expansion in the 1990s and 2000s was a mistake, and that it propelled us toward the unhappy situation NATO finds itself in vis-à-vis an aggressive and acquisitive Russia.

    According to recent reports, I agree of course that Vladimir Putin would like the geographical disposition of NATO as it existed in 1997 but very much not its order of battle. But Michael sees the growth of NATO’s membership as unwieldy and strategically burdensome in light of the reduced military footprint of the alliance. I don’t think that’s right. Rather, the increased size of NATO and its reduced manpower were related and, more importantly, could be seen as strategically offsetting developments.

    Daniel Foster is a contributing editor at National Review.

    On “Strategic Depth for Thee, Not for Me?”.

    Ryanair Now Withholds Free Seats Until Just Before Departure, Blames Customer Feedback

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1017 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that ryanair has quietly updated its policy for how it assigns seats to those people who don’t pay the seat assignment fee, as reported by The Irish Times.
    • Recent findings suggest that ryanair is known for being an unapologetic ultra low cost carrier.
    • However, the way the airline is randomly allocating seats has quietly changed as of late October 2026, coinciding with the start of the winter schedule.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that ryanair has quietly updated its policy for how it assigns seats to those people who don’t pay the seat assignment fee, as reported by The Irish Times. While I wouldn’t consider this to be anything unreasonable, what I’m amused by is the carrier’s justification. The airline claims that it’s doing this due to customer feedback, rather than to generate more revenue.

    Recent findings suggest that ryanair is known for being an unapologetic ultra low cost carrier. The airline has low base fares, and then charges fees for just about everything. Among other things, the airline charges to assign seats in advance, and those who don’t pay for specific seat assignments are just randomly assigned seats (and often in a rather punitive way).

    However, the way the airline is randomly allocating seats has quietly changed as of late October 2026, coinciding with the start of the winter schedule. Historically, the airline has automatically assigned seats to passengers without seat assignments around 24 hours before departure.

    Recent findings suggest that some passengers seemed to “game” this, and would essentially “gamble.” What they’d do is wait until 24 hours out to see what seat they were assigned for free. Then if they weren’t happy with their automatic seat assignment, they could still pay to assign a better seat.

    Industry observers note that under the upcoming policy, the airline still issues a boarding pass up to 24 hours out, but without a seat assignment. Then the boarding pass automatically shows the seat assignment within four hours of departure.

    The logic here seems pretty clear — some people do care somewhat about where they sit, but want to avoid fees if they can. By withholding seat assignments until hours before departure, passengers are presumably more likely to pay for seat assignments in advance, to avoid that uncertainty.

    Ryanair has confirmed this seat assignment policy change in a statement, sharing that “the timing of the allocation of free random seats is determined at all times by the airline.” Right, nobody disputes that the airline has the right to do this.

    So, what’s the logic for this policy change? According to the airline, it’s “to allow those passengers who wish to select their preferred seat more time to do so. We had a number of complaints this summer that passengers could not book their preferred seat on the day of travel as it had been already randomly allocated as a free seat up to 24 hours prior to departure.”.

    The Ryanair representative went on to say that “passengers who choose a free of charge random seat clearly don’t mind where they sit, and their digital boarding pass is automatically updated between three to four hours prior to departure, which is well before they arrive at either their departure airport or their boarding gate.”.

    Ryanair is of course within its rights to have this policy, but I think the logic is pretty obvious, and it’s to generate more revenue. After all, 24 hours out people would see what they were randomly assigned at online check-in, and would still have a lot of choices if they wanted to pay for seats, since most people don’t check-in online exactly at the 24-hour mark.

    But within a few hours of departure, virtually everyone has checked in online, and not many seats will be left. So I imagine the goal is to condition more customers to pay for seat assignments in advance. I love the claim that customers complained that their preferred seats on the day of travel were randomly allocated to others for free:.

    According to recent reports, ryanair has a new policy for automatic seat allocations. In the past, the airline would automatically assign seats to passengers 24 hours out, giving them quite the window to “gamble” on the free seat assignment, and then pay for a different seat assignment if they weren’t happy with the free one.

    The airline has now started only assigning free seats at most four hours out. The airline claims that this is due to customer feedback, so that passengers have more time to assign their choice of paid seats. However, I imagine that’s not quite accurate, and this is instead about conditioning people to pay for seat assignments, rather than “gambling” on the free allocations.

    What do you make of this Ryanair seating policy change?

    @DKB same in the UK, waiting till the last few hours often got you row 1 or an exit row for nothing. That's clearly what they're closing off. Families with under 12s are less affected, kids get free reserved seats once one adult pays for a seat.

    I can't imagine choosing Ryanair unless I wanted a bus ride.
