    Tech Report: At the Races: The fresh Trump Democrats

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1938 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Editor’s note: At the Races will not publish next week on Thanksgiving Day.
    • By Niels Lesniewski, Mary Ellen McIntire and Daniela Altimari.
    • Senate Democrats powered their way to a majority by flipping nine seats – their biggest gain in nearly 70 years.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Editor’s note: At the Races will not publish next week on Thanksgiving Day. We’ll be back the following week.

    By Niels Lesniewski, Mary Ellen McIntire and Daniela Altimari.

    Senate Democrats powered their way to a majority by flipping nine seats – their biggest gain in nearly 70 years.

    Eight of those wins were in states that Donald Trump has carried every time he’s run so it’s no surprise that some of the incoming senators are talking up the prospect of working with him over the next two years.

    “We don't have time to wait until we have a different administration in the White House,” South Carolina Sen.-elect Annie Andrews told reporters this week. “We have two years ahead of us. We have very real problems that we need to address.”.

    Andrews is the first Democrat elected to the Senate from South Carolina since 1998. A pediatrician, she cited reducing prescription drug costs as a potential area of common ground with Trump.

    “I support the president's attempts to stop taxes on tips and taxes on Social Security,” Andrews stated, citing two selling points of last year’s GOP reconciliation law. During the campaign, she issued a policy paper expressing support for making those provisions of the tax code permanent.

    James Talarico, the incoming senator from Texas, told fellow Democrats gathered in Denver last week that if Trump wanted “the same plaques and portraits and busts as LBJ, we can help make that a reality.”.

    “We should make the final two years of his presidency the most productive of any presidency in American history,” said Talarico, the first Democrat in nearly 40 years to win a Senate race in the Lone Star State.

    The idea of Trump and congressional Democrats working together might seem far-fetched, but with the incoming Democrats hailing from places such as Alaska, the Carolinas, Mississippi, Kansas and Texas, there’s a political incentive to appeal to Republican-leaning voters back home.

    But intentionally or not, Talarico and other newly elected Democrats might be borrowing from the playbook of New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who has welcomed Trump when goals align, including on an effort to redevelop the Sunnyside rail yard in the president’s native Queens.

    Trump has stressed that he will veto legislation he opposes from the incoming Democratic Congress, but, at least for the moment, he seems open to deals.

    “I have a feeling that this is going to be an unbelievably productive two years,” Trump told Fox News early Thursday morning in Shenzhen, China, adding that  he would invite Democrats to the White House.

    According to recent reports, “I respect them,” he said. “Politics is a nasty game, and they won.”.

    Peltola prevails: Former Rep. Mary Peltola’s victory over Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska brings the Senate Democratic Caucus to 56 seats in the 120th Congress. Peltola finished with just over 50 percent of the vote, negating the need to use the state’s ranked choice voting system. The race for the state’s at-large House district was decided by a ranked choice tally, with Republican Rep. Nick Begich defeating independent Bill Hill 51 percent to 49 percent in the final round. Alaska voters also rejected an attempt to eliminate ranked choice voting in the state by a vote of 54 percent to 46 percent.

    Sources indicate that leadership elections: House Democrats nominated Hakeem Jeffries to serve as the next speaker in a 251-11 closed-door Wednesday vote, Roll Call’s Lauren Green reports. That puts Jeffries in prime position to become the first Black speaker when the full chamber votes in January. Meanwhile, Senate Democrats are scheduled to pick the next majority leader on Dec. 1, as our colleague Savannah Behrmann reports. Charles E. Schumer, who’s being challenged by Maryland’s Chris Van Hollen, maintains he has the votes to win.

    A victory lap and a warning: Even as the Congressional Hispanic Caucus celebrates its largest roster ever, the group’s leaders had a warning for their fellow Democrats: “Latino voters gave Democrats a two-year lease, but it expires in 2028 unless the party changes its playbook for good,” said California Rep. Linda T. Sánchez, who leads the group’s campaign arm.

    Recent findings suggest that #KYGOV: Republican Rep. James R. Comer, who was just elected to a sixth full term, rolled out his much-anticipated run for Kentucky governor this week. The Bluegrass State is one of three states holding statewide executive  elections in 2027, along with Louisiana and Mississippi.

    Industry observers note that rocky Mountain roundup: Rep. Lauren Boebert, an outspoken Republican with a national reputation as a Second Amendment provocateur, lost her bid for reelection in Colorado’s 4th District to Democrat Eileen Laubacher, a retired Navy rear admiral. Meanwhile, Republican Gabe Evans, who fell short in his bid for a second term in the neighboring 8th District, confirmed he prepares to challenge Laubacher in two years, Roll Call’s Samantha Freeman reports.

    It has been revealed that they’re back: Our colleague Nina Heller tracked down former congressional staffers who are back on the Hill as newly elected members. “I never thought this would be the path, but I’m honored to do it,” remarked Rep.-elect Sydney Gruters, who worked for fellow Florida Republicans Greg Steube and Vern Buchanan, her soon-to-be House predecessor.

    RIP: Former Rep. Jim McDermott, a longtime advocate for universal health care, died last week at the age of 89. The Washington Democrat, who retired to a small town in southwestern France after 28 years in the House, was hailed by his home state’s senior senator, Patty Murray, “as one of the first and most powerful voices fighting to fix our broken health care system in Congress.”.

    Where the House stands: As of 3 p.m. Eastern time, House Democrats have flipped 46 seats to three for the Republicans and are on track to hold at least 257 seats in the next Congress. Six races remain uncalled by The Associated Press, including two in Louisiana that will be decided by December runoffs. The AP is also yet to call Tennessee’s 4th District, where Republican Rep. Scott DesJarlais has conceded to Democrat Victoria Broderick, who leads by 272 votes out of nearly 200,000 cast.

    It has been revealed that thompson loses: California Rep. Mike Thompson lost his bid for a 15th term to former venture capitalist Eric Jones, a political newcomer who poured millions into his campaign. Thompson is the second California member to lose to a fellow Democrat this year, after Rep. Jimmy Gomez. But Rep. Doris Matsui held off an intraparty challenge from democratic socialist Mai Vang.

    2028 draft: Supporters of former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg launched Team Pete PAC on Thursday, an effort to urge him to launch a second presidential bid.

    Battleground rep: Michigan Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet will be House Democrats' battleground leadership representative in the next Congress, acting as a bridge between members in competitive districts and party leadership. McDonald Rivet, who ran unopposed for the position, will succeed Nevada Rep. Susie Lee.

    #INGOV: Indiana Gov. Mike Braun launched his 2028 reelection campaign as speculation swirls that state Attorney General Todd Rokita could challenge him for the Republican nomination. Rokita, a former congressman, has criticized Braun for not disciplining state educators who posted controversial comments after Charlie Kirk’s assassination but mentioned last week that he wanted Braun to “run for governor” and “be successful.” The two previously faced off in a 2018 Republican Senate primary, with Braun going on to serve one term in the Senate.

    Newly introduced leader for New Dems: Illinois Rep. Nikki Budzinski will chair the New Democrat Coalition next year, taking over from fellow Illinois Rep. Brad Schneider. New Mexico’s Gabe Vasquez, Ohio’s Greg Landsman and Washington’s Kim Schrier and Marilyn Strickland will serve as co-chairs of the center-left group, the largest ideological entity in the Democratic Caucus.

    In a recent development, remembering Holden: Former Pennsylvania Rep. Tim Holden, who served 10 terms in the House before losing a Democratic primary to Matt Cartwright in 2012, died Sunday at the age of 69. House members held a moment of silence for Holden on the floor Thursday. Republican Rep. Dan Meuser, whose district includes territory Holden once represented, described him as “well-liked and widely respected, including by those on both sides of the political aisle.”.

    Investigated: Ohio Rep.-elect Brian Poindexter is under investigation for alleged sexual harassment after the Democrat’s campaign hired a human resources firm to investigate the complaint. Both the Blue Dog PAC and the Congressional Progressive Caucus, which had endorsed Poindexter’s candidacy, dropped their support in the closing days of the campaign after learning of the allegation.

    It has been revealed that tennessee two-step: Tennessee Democrat Jeri Green, who narrowly lost the open governor’s race to Republican Sen. Marsha Blackburn, revealed a bid for the state Senate seat GOP Rep.-elect Brent Taylor is expected to vacate. Taylor narrowly defeated Democratic state Rep. Justin Pearson in the redrawn 9th District, though both men were simultaneously reelected to their legislative seats.

    The  historic “blue tsunami” that swept Democrats into commanding Senate and House majorities has some pundits questioning whether Republicans will ever be in charge again, observes Roll Call elections analyst Nathan L. Gonzales of Inside Elections.

    But you just have to look at the election results from two years ago to realize that when it comes to winning party coalitions, nothing is permanent anymore, Nathan writes.

    Only the young: Fresh York magazine catches up with young Republicans in South Carolina and finds that immigration policy and the war in Iran have turned many of the MAGA faithful against the GOP.

    From satirist to senator: The Washington Post traces South Carolina Democrat Annie Andrews’ journey from an online agitator who made relentless fun of Republicans to a newly elected senator who says she’s eager to work with her GOP colleagues.

    Bad blood: The Boston Globe explores the long-standing rivalry between Maine’s two newest members of Congress: Democratic Sen.-elect Troy Jackson and Republican Rep.-elect Paul LePage.

    Schumer’s choice: Uncertainty around whether Schumer will seek another term in 2028 has risen as the Fresh York Democrat seeks to become Senate majority leader next year, Politico reports.

    That's how long it's been since the Senate Democratic Caucus last saw a contested race for its top leadership position, with Maryland’s Van Hollen now challenging Schumer for the job.

    Recent findings suggest that after Democrats lost eight Senate seats (and their majority) in the 1994 Republican Revolution, 42-year old South Dakota Sen. Tom Daschle edged out Connecticut's Christopher J. Dodd by a single vote, 24-23, to succeed outgoing leader George Mitchell of Maine.

    The last time a sitting Democratic Senate leader faced a formal challenge was a decade earlier, in 1984.

    West Virginia's Robert C. Byrd, who’d been leading his party in the chamber since 1977, easily fended off a bid by Florida’s Lawton Chiles.

    The last time either party experienced a contested race for the position was four years ago, when Florida Sen. Rick Scott challenged Republican leader Mitch McConnell of Kentucky.

    As Byrd did before him, McConnell handily defeated his challenger in the secret-ballot vote.

    Recent findings suggest that machine recounts in a pair of House races in North Carolina are expected to be completed Monday. Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx trails Democrat Chuck Hubbard by 331 votes, while GOP Rep. Pat Harrigan leads Democratic challenger Ashley Bell by just over 2,500 votes. The trailing candidate could then request a partial hand recount.

    Monday is also the deadline for Republican Rep. Brad Finstad to formally request a recount in his razor-thin race against Democrat Jake Johnson in Minnesota’s 1st District. Finstad, who reportedly said he’ll seek one, trails Johnson by 321 votes.

    Mobile Passport Control: Free App That Speeds Up US Immigration

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1290 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Frequent travelers to the United States are probably familiar with Global Entry, which allows enrolled members to get expedited immigration at US airports.
    • According to recent reports, if you don’t want Global Entry (or aren’t eligible), your next best option is Mobile Passport Control.
    • Mobile Passport Control (MPC) is a free app that allows travelers to submit their travel document, photo, and customs declaration information, before they arrive at the immigration checkpoint at a US airport.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Frequent travelers to the United States are probably familiar with Global Entry, which allows enrolled members to get expedited immigration at US airports. However, applying for Global Entry is a bit of a process, and there’s a cost to participate.

    According to recent reports, if you don’t want Global Entry (or aren’t eligible), your next best option is Mobile Passport Control. This is sort of a hidden program that doesn’t get talked about enough, given that it can significantly cut down your wait times at US immigration. In this post, I’d like to talk about how this works, as I’ve used it a couple of times now (when traveling internationally with our younger son, who doesn’t yet have Global Entry).

    Mobile Passport Control (MPC) is a free app that allows travelers to submit their travel document, photo, and customs declaration information, before they arrive at the immigration checkpoint at a US airport.

    Industry observers note that travelers just have to download the app, which is available for Apple and Android. The idea is that the app streamlines the traveler’s entry process to the United States by reducing passport control inspection times and overall wait times.

    Those who use MPC can access a separate immigration screening checkpoint. Really that’s the biggest advantage — because not many people use this program (as of now), the wait times are generally much shorter than the standard wait times.

    There are some vital things to be aware of, as you’d expect:.

    In the interest of being thorough, here are the current airports participating in Mobile Passport Control:.

    Recent findings suggest that the Mobile Passport Control app couldn’t be much easier to use. I’d recommend downloading the app prior to boarding your flight to the United States, and completing the basic requirements. Then you have to submit your customs declaration after you land in the United States (within four hours of when you intend to clear immigration).

    Once you download the app, there are several pages explaining how the app works, plus you have to agree to a disclaimer statement.

    After that you can go through steps required for a particular entry to the country. Note that you can use one app to submit your application for multiple people in the same family. Furthermore, you can save the passport details in the app for multiple trips, eliminating the need to submit all of this information each time (though you do need to make a customs declaration each time).

    To start the process, you’ll have to state which CBP port you’ll be arriving at, and they all show on a dropdown menu.

    Recent findings suggest that at that point you’ll have to select the travelers who will be entering the country. If you’ve already saved people to your profile, they’ll show on that page. Otherwise you can start from scratch, which just requires scanning the document, and then all the information will be auto-populated.

    You’ll then need to capture traveler photos. This doesn’t need to be a passport-quality photo — you just have to follow some very basic guidelines, like removing hats and sunglasses, and making sure only one person’s face is visible.

    The above can all be saved to your profile. However, what you do need to complete with each trip is answering six standard CBP declaration questions.

    You’ll only want to submit this when you arrive at your point of entry in the United States. The app asks you to submit this once you’ve arrived at the airport, though in reality you have up to four hours to go through immigration from the time that your application is submitted.

    Once you submit your document, you’ll be given a receipt with a QR code, which you’ll need to scan when you see an immigration officer.

    Once you land at your US point of entry and arrive in the immigration hall, look for the Mobile Passport Control signage. This will bring you to an area separate from the standard US immigration line.

    You still need to queue to see an immigration officer, and when you get to the officer, you’ll see a scanning device where you should scan your QR code. The benefit is that this line is usually much shorter, and also that you generally won’t be asked as many questions (since you’ve already answered some questions via the app).

    Both times I’ve gone through the MPC lane, the wait was less than five minutes, while the general immigration line looked much longer. The main benefit of MPC isn’t even the time savings from getting some of the work done in advance through the app, but rather just having access to a shorter line.

    Recent findings suggest that mobile Passport Control isn’t as good as Global Entry, plain and simple. With Global Entry there’s almost never a wait, you just have to look at the camera, an officer acknowledges you, and then you’re usually sent on your way. The Mobile Passport Control experience isn’t as seamless. However, it’s the next best thing.

    There’s no enrollment cost, using the app takes maybe a few minutes to set up, and then with each trip it just takes a minute or so to answer the declaration questions. Getting access to a special immigration line for that is awesome, as it could potentially save you a significant amount of time.

    Recent findings suggest that of course like many things in life, I imagine that as this app becomes more popular and well known, it will also become less useful. After all, when everyone gets access to a special lane, no one gets access to a special lane. 😉.

    Mobile Passport Control is an awesome free app that can save you time at US immigration. The app is easy to use, and allows you to submit your documents and customs declaration prior to speaking to an immigration officer. Most valuable of all, those with MPC get access to a special lane at immigration, which is typically much shorter than the standard one.

    While I’d still recommend Global Entry, those who don’t have it should use MPC if they’re eligible.

    Have you ever used Mobile Passport Control before? If so, what was your experience like?

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    This week, Soneil Spark rolls out its Mobile Battery Energy Storage System (Mobile BESS), the portable, modular battery storage built into a towable trailer.

    The company, offering bespoke, modular energy solutions, is introducing Mobile BESS at RE+ 2026. It delivers temporary backup and off-grid power, working with what’s available by taking power from the grid, a generator, or solar.

    Recent findings suggest that “Wherever your business goes, the power goes with it. Simply tow it where energy demand grows,” said Sonya Jain, CEO of Soneil Spark, in a statement. “Start with one unit and add more as your needs change.”.

    Recent findings suggest that it’s a simple set up, the tech giant said. Mobile BESS works with no crane, no trenching, and no utility wait. That makes it a natural fit for a job site which may be months away from permanent service, a film set or event that can’t tolerate generator noise and fumes, a utility crew restoring power after a storm, or a remote mine or farm beyond the grid’s reach.

    It has been revealed that on sites that already run generators, the Mobile BESS syncs with them to cover peaks and start-up gaps, so the generators run fewer hours. Where diesel is restricted, it offers a quiet alternative.

    Where containerized storage is built to be placed once, the Mobile BESS is built to be towed and to work in any weather. It includes:.

    Sources indicate that the Mobile BESS is built for generator and equipment rental, construction, emergency and backup power, utilities, electrical contractors, events, film and entertainment, and off-grid sites such as mining and agriculture. A hybrid option adds EV charging.

    Royal Air Maroc Business Class Boeing 787 Review: The World’s Worst Flat Bed?

    ⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that to finish off the return portion of our Orient Express adventure via Africa trip, we flew Royal Air Maroc’s Boeing 787-8 business class on the 8hr25min flight from Casablanca (CMN) to Miami (MIA).
    • Recent findings suggest that the version of Royal Air Maroc’s 787 that we flew had what I’d consider to be the world’s worst flat bed business class seat.
    • Sources indicate that to Royal Air Maroc’s credit, the airline is on balance the best northern African carrier, in my opinion.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that to finish off the return portion of our Orient Express adventure via Africa trip, we flew Royal Air Maroc’s Boeing 787-8 business class on the 8hr25min flight from Casablanca (CMN) to Miami (MIA). While the flight operated relatively on schedule, it otherwise had quite some room for improvement.

    Recent findings suggest that the version of Royal Air Maroc’s 787 that we flew had what I’d consider to be the world’s worst flat bed business class seat. When you combine that with no Wi-Fi and incredibly lackluster service, it’s hard to praise the airline too much.

    Sources indicate that to Royal Air Maroc’s credit, the airline is on balance the best northern African carrier, in my opinion. And the flight attendant working our part of the cabin was at least well intentioned. The food was relatively decent as well. It also has to be pointed out that Royal Air Maroc’s 787s have four different types of configurations, and these seats are limited to most of the 787-8s (while the 787-9s have better seats).

    So while I have a hard time giving Royal Air Maroc too much credit for our experience, I also view the airline in a better light than carriers like Air Algerie, for example.

    Ford and I booked an itinerary on Royal Air Maroc all the way from Malaga to Miami via Casablanca. The reason was because the airline offered the best schedule that would get us home the same day after our Orient Express Sailing Yachts cruise.

    Royal Air Maroc often makes only one business class seat available, so I had to get a bit creative to make this work. I ended up booking one ticket using 57,500 American AAdvantage miles plus $85.72 in taxes & fees, while the other ticket was booked with cash, at the cost of $1,620, with the following itinerary:.

    10/09 AT989 Malaga to Casablanca departing 2:15PM arriving 1:30PM10/09 AT204 Casablanca to Miami departing 3:00PM arriving 7:45PM.

    Obviously paying cash for a ticket wasn’t ideal, but that still ended up being less out of pocket than flying British Airways business class through London on awards, factoring in the carrier surcharges.

    Sources indicate that we had a fairly short connection in Casablanca, as we had just arrived in Royal Air Maroc’s 737 business class from Malaga. We first had to clear transit security, which only took a few minutes. While we would’ve had access to Royal Air Maroc’s lounge, we didn’t really have much time, so we headed straight to our departure gate.

    According to recent reports, our flight was departing from gate A10, with boarding scheduled for 2:10PM, 50 minutes before departure. As is common for US-bound flights, the departure area was roped off from the rest of the terminal, and there were some boarding pass checks. However, we weren’t subjected to extra screening (I assume that’s just for those with “SSSS” on their boarding pass).

    I must admit, Royal Air Maroc’s livery is pretty beautiful, no?

    I also have an embarrassing confession to make. Boarding started a few minutes ahead of the published 2:10PM time, and I attempted to board… only to find out that I was accidentally attempting to board the flight to New York. Gate A9 and A10 are right next to one another, the monitor was tiny, etc. In fairness, I wasn’t the only person attempting to board the wrong flight, so it seems like that could maybe be organized a little better. 😉.

    Anyway, boarding did end up starting right on schedule, with wheelchair passengers being invited to board first, followed by business class passengers and oneworld elite members.

    Royal Air Maroc’s Boeing 787-8 business class takes up the entire space between the first and second set of doors. It consists of 18 seats, spread across three rows, in a 2-2-2 configuration. We were in seats 2A and 2C, the window and aisle seat in the second row on the left side.

    Royal Air Maroc has the Stelia Equinox 3D seat, which like I remarked, is the worst flat bed business class in the world, in my opinion. I just don’t understand what the designer of this seat was thinking.

    I understand that in theory this is supposed to be a high density layout, but with just 18 seats in that space, it’s hardly efficient — American has 20 reverse herringbone seats in the same space on the same plane (though admittedly on Royal Air Maroc the lavatories are also in front of the second set of doors, so it’s not a fully fair comparison).

    According to recent reports, what makes these seats so bad? Well, basically everything. The seats completely lack storage, and they have the most bizarre top/bottom configuration when you recline your seat. Fortunately I was traveling with Ford (no one I’d rather be in these top/bottom seats with!), but if next to a stranger, these are just downright bad.

    In a recent development, where do we even begin? For one, these seats have the padding (and look) of an ironing board. So the comfort is definitely lacking.

    Ford had never been in these kinds of seats before, and as he sat down and looked forward, he was genuinely confused by how the ottomans were at completely different levels — that’s understandable confusion!

    It has been revealed that in this configuration, the tray tables fold out from the center side of the seat, and are so poorly designed. They basically refuse to stay in place, and if they move even just a little, they sort of “plop” down, as they go off the edge of the little “holder.”.

    Then there’s the whole console between seats, where you’ll find a panel with the seat controls, a headphone jack, an entertainment controller, an AC power outlet, and a USB-A outlet (there’s no USB-C or wireless charging).

    Industry observers note that the seat just completely lacks when it comes to storage and comfort, as there’s not really anywhere practical to place things. For example, if you have your laptop out and then the meal service starts, where are you supposed to place it? There’s nowhere to put it, other than the floor.

    Perhaps the one positive thing I can say about this Royal Air Maroc hard product is that there were individual air nozzles, which at least helped with being able to regulate the feeling of being too warm.

    I’m not trying to be sarcastic, but I do consider this to be the world’s worst flat bed business class. On the plus side, I guess at least it’s not angled (is that really a thing anymore?), and the version of this seat on Philippine Airlines A330s is worse.

    Recent findings suggest that royal Air Maroc’s 787 business class has 18.5″ seat back entertainment screens, with audio and video on demand. The system was far from cutting edge and the selection wasn’t massive, but it also wasn’t terrible. There was a decent selection of movies, TV demonstrates, music, games, and of course the map feature.

    In a recent development, I tried my best to count the number of entertainment options, and I got to around 230 movies, so that’s not a bad selection. However, the options also weren’t terribly modern, for the most part.

    Unfortunately there was no Wi-Fi on this plane, which is pretty uncompetitive nowadays. The good news is that Royal Air Maroc aims to introduce Starlink Wi-Fi in 2027, so that’ll be a major upgrade.

    When it comes to Royal Air Maroc business class amenities, a pillow and blanket were waiting at my seat upon boarding. The blanket was cozy without being overly luxurious or warm, while the pillow was fine, but a little on the small side.

    Industry observers note that later on in the flight I discovered there were also mattress pads in the overhead bin, but go figure that no crew member ever informed any passenger of this (let alone offered to make beds), which is such a missed opportunity. How sad when the airline invests in something like that, but it’s totally wasted, as I didn’t see a single passenger using these.

    Headphones were also waiting at each seat, but they were very much on the cheap side, and didn’t have good noise cancelation, and also weren’t very comfortable.

    Amenity kits had been placed at the seats before boarding, and were fine. I kind of liked the Royal Air Maroc branding on the kit as such. In terms of contents, there were socks, eyeshades, a dental kit, and a small selection of products from Moroccan skincare brand Nectarome.

    During boarding, the crew came around with pre-departure drinks, including the choice of lemon mint juice or water, followed by warm towels.

    The menu and drink list for the flight were also distributed.

    Sources indicate that there were no slippers or pajamas. All-in-all, the amenities were okay. They weren’t terrible, but also weren’t memorable.

    In a recent development, boarding took a rather long time, as the flight was full. The main cabin door closed at 3:10PM, 10 minutes after our scheduled departure time. At that point the safety video was screened, which was interesting to watch.

    At 3:15PM we began our pushback, and then at 3:25PM we began our taxi.

    We had a brief taxi out to runway 35R, where we had to hold for a few minutes. We were cleared for takeoff at 3:40PM, and rocketed off into the afternoon sky. The views on the climb out were lovely, and the seatbelt sign was turned off around five minutes after takeoff.

    Once we leveled off, we had around eight hours remaining to Miami.

    In business class on this Royal Air Maroc flight, the main meal was served after takeoff, while a snack was served before landing. In theory the menu talked about how there was dine on demand.

    It has been revealed that I’m sure that could’ve been requested, but that’s not something the crew ever offered — they just took meal orders before takeoff, and then served everyone the main meal after takeoff. Much like with the mattress pads, it just seems like there’s a gap between what they’re trying to go for, and what they’re actually offering.

    You can find the Royal Air Maroc business class menu and drink list below.

    The first round of drinks were served around 35 minutes after takeoff, so credit to the airline for the speed at which the first drink was served, plus the overall presentation.

    Industry observers note that I had a glass of the Moroccan white wine. That was served with a canapé consisting of sweet chili prawn with sesame seeds, smoked salmon rose, and a foie gras mousse bite, along with two packaged snacks (cheese biscuits and roasted salted almonds).

    Industry observers note that that was a lovely start to the meal, but Ford had less luck. He ordered a Diet Coke, and when he opened the can, it exploded. I understand the concept of cans sometimes having problems, but I’ve never seen anything like this before.

    Recent findings suggest that it wasn’t just that an ounce or two immediately sprayed out, but instead, within two seconds, there was no liquid left in the can, and instead, it was all over him and the cabin. I don’t even understand how that could happen. So it took quite a while for us to clean up that mess.

    It has been revealed that there were three options for starters. I ordered the tuna tataki with mixed lettuce, mango, and wasabi cream, while Ford had the harira and dates (for the record, I would’ve gone for the more Moroccan option as well, but wanted to give Ford his first choice, and get pictures of different things). Both were quite decent, but nothing great.

    Eventually our appetizers were cleared, and then our mains were brought out. I had the grilled sea bass with chimichurri sauce, with quinoa, lentils, and mushrooms, while Ford had the beef tajine with prunes, dried apricot, and almonds. Both dishes were fine — the fish surprisingly lacked flavor, and the beef tajine was just okay, not bad, but not as good as you’d hope for the flag carrier of a country.

    After the main course, there was the choice of a couple of desserts, fruit, or cheese. Ford and I each ordered one of the desserts (cheesecake and a pastry with amlou), and then split a cheese plate.

    Sources indicate that all-in-all, the meal wasn’t bad, and wrapped up within two hours of departure. The challenge was more the service. I understand based on the above pictures, everything actually looks pretty decent and organized. But the crew had a complete inability to offer drink refills and remove plates, even when specifically requested. It wasn’t that they weren’t nice, they were just really disorganized and slow with responding to requests.

    For example, below is what Ford’s tray looked like when we were having the cheese course. You’d think they could’ve cleared something, but nope, they just kind of looked at it. I’ll talk more about service later, but getting a drink refill was quite the undertaking.

    In a recent development, royal Air Maroc’s 787 business class lavatory situation is a bit confusing. There’s one lavatory at the very front of the cabin, but it seems to be reserved for the crew. At least that’s the impression I had, as that’s what the flight attendants suggested to me.

    There were then two lavatories behind business class, but the one on the left (on my aisle) was for economy (so the curtain was hung around it accordingly), while the one on the right (the other aisle) was for business class.

    Sources indicate that one lavatory for 18 business class passengers isn’t ideal. The issue isn’t the ratio as such, but instead, if one person is using the lavatory for an extended period, you’re kind of just locked out. The bigger issue is that going from the left aisle to the back right requires either going through the economy galley or forward galley, and the crew didn’t seem thrilled by traffic there.

    Anyway, the lavatory as such was a standard Dreamliner one, so wasn’t half bad. And while I wouldn’t say it was clean, it also wasn’t filthy.

    Industry observers note that once back at my seat, we reclined both of the seats to get some rest. This is where you really realize how absurd these seats are. Imagine you’re sitting in one of these seats next to a stranger, or imagine if you’re in the “top” seat and want to sleep, while the person in the “bottom” seat doesn’t. The person in the “top” seat is basically hanging over you.

    Since we were traveling together, this wasn’t a huge deal, but I just can’t believe anyone thought this would be a good seat standard on a long haul flight.

    With no Wi-Fi and not a whole lot to do, we tried to get some rest. We fell asleep with around 6hr30min remaining to Miami, while approaching the Azores….

    …and we woke up with around two hours remaining.

    In a recent development, honestly, that was some very good rest for me on a plane, since I’m usually a terrible sleeper. And while I’d love to credit the seat, the truth is that just not knowing what to do with yourself really helps with getting some rest. I knew I couldn’t be productive, there wasn’t much on the entertainment system for me to enjoy, etc.

    It has been revealed that the crew served the pre-landing snack around 90 minutes before landing, and there were two choices. One choice was a salmon sandwich and tandoori chicken sandwich, and the other choice was a beef burger and chicken burger, and we had one of each. That was served with a side of yogurt with almonds, dates, and amlou.

    I didn’t find it to be a terribly large meal, but it was sufficient.

    In addition to water, I accompanied the meal with a mint tea, which was relatively nicely presented.

    Compared to Air Algerie, service on Royal Air Maroc was excellent… but that’s about all I can say. To the crew’s credit, they were relatively charming, and smiled every once in a while. So friendliness wasn’t the problem.

    According to recent reports, instead, the problem was just how reactive service was. If there was an empty glass, they’d just look at it, rather than removing it, or offering a refill. And even if you asked for a refill during a meal, it would take 15 minutes for it to happen. As another example, with the pre-landing meal, they never proactively asked anyone if they wanted something to drink — they just poured water, and that was it (though they were happy to fulfill requests). These just seem like basic things that should be fixed.

    This felt like assembly line service to the max, in terms of the service flow being about what was convenient for the crew, rather than what passengers wanted.

    At around 7:15PM Miami time, the captain was on the PA to announce that we’d soon start descending, and would be landing in around 45 minutes. Our approach ended up stretching on quite a bit, as we flew down the coast of Florida, before flying out over the Everglades, and then turning around.

    We ended up touching down in Miami at 8PM, on runway 9. While we got off the runway very close to our arrival gate, we ended up just holding position for around 15 minutes on a taxiway, with no update from the pilots. We finally pulled into our gate at 8:20PM.

    We rapidly cleared immigration and customs, and were excited to be heading home, wrapping up a fun and memorable trip!

    According to recent reports, I can’t complain too much about our Royal Air Maroc 787 business class flight. We were close to on time, the crew wasn’t unfriendly, and since I was traveling with Ford, I didn’t mind these seats. The food also wasn’t bad.

    However, when compared to other business class experiences, there’s definitely huge room for improvement. These seats are really quite uncompetitive, the lack of Wi-Fi was disappointing, and the service was just lacking. Royal Air Maroc will soon introduce Starlink Wi-Fi and is also introducing upgraded business class seats, and I feel like if they invested a bit in service training, they could really be a very competitive airline.

    I’d say that by regional standards, Royal Air Maroc is still the best carrier in northern Africa. But that’s not to say that there isn’t (substantial) room for improvement.

    What do you make of Royal Air Maroc’s 787 business class?

    At his DealBook interview with Andrew Ross Sorkin last week, Palmer Luckey, founder of AI weapon producer Anduril, made a clear case for the American defense sector, one based on recognizing that our society is protected by physical military power, that America is fundamentally good and deserving of this protection, and that the rest of the world benefits from a muscular (and not necessarily confrontational) America. He argued that we have to be realistic about the fact that “peace through strength” means being able to present a credible threat of retaliatory violence to would-be adversaries and that these actions support a constrained and functional government.

    It’s not often that we hear contentious positions on American strength explained without cartoonish warrior-posturing. It is refreshing.

    Skyler Safriet is a William F. Buckley Jr. Fellow in Political Journalism for National Review. She is a graduate of Boston College, where she studied philosophy and competed as a heptathlete in track and field.

    House Ethics panel adopts changes aimed at speeding up investigations

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that ethics Chairman Michael Guest, left, and ranking member Mark DeSaulnier arrive for a committee meeting on Capitol Hill in April.
    • In a year roiled by sexual misconduct allegations in the House, the Ethics Committee approved a series of changes Thursday that its members say are intended to improve how the panel handles its investigations.
    • In a rare public meeting lasting less than 10 minutes, the committee discussed proposed tweaks aimed at speeding up its processes, after some observers have criticized its pace.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that ethics Chairman Michael Guest, left, and ranking member Mark DeSaulnier arrive for a committee meeting on Capitol Hill in April. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    In a year roiled by sexual misconduct allegations in the House, the Ethics Committee approved a series of changes Thursday that its members say are intended to improve how the panel handles its investigations.

    In a rare public meeting lasting less than 10 minutes, the committee discussed proposed tweaks aimed at speeding up its processes, after some observers have criticized its pace.

    In a recent development, “My problem with the Ethics Committee is it just takes too damn long,” Rep. Madeleine Dean, D-Pa., said earlier this year.

    The internal rule changes were adopted in a voice vote by the committee, which is evenly divided between Republicans and Democrats.

    Industry observers note that “We believe that these rule changes will provide more transparency. They will expedite our investigative process while maintaining protections for witnesses and victims, while also making sure that … due process is protected,” Chair Michael Guest, R-Miss., noted during the meeting.

    It has been revealed that when former Reps. Eric Swalwell, D-Calif., and Tony Gonzales, R-Texas, resigned earlier this year amid misconduct allegations, it sparked outrage as some called to rethink how the House polices bad behavior. Both men were on the radar of the Ethics Committee at the time, but such investigations have tended to move slowly.

    Sources indicate that “I want the Ethics Committee to move faster,” stated panel member Rep. Suhas Subramanyam, D-Va., back in April.

    The committee did not immediately make available the exact text of the changes it adopted Thursday. But a summary sent in a news release earlier this week included one proposal aimed at “consolidating deadlines” for a member to respond to an investigative subcommittee’s findings. Another tweak aimed at speeding things up would give the chair and ranking member subpoena power on behalf of the committee, rather than requiring a full committee vote.

    The summary described “codifying the Committee’s policy of publicly disclosing any findings that a Member engaged in sexual harassment or other sexual misconduct” while “prohibiting publication of the identity of any victim.”.

    Also on the list: “Expanding the circumstances under which fines and denials of privileges are considered an appropriate sanction to include any abuses of position.”.

    Recent findings suggest that it comes as women on both sides of the aisle have formed a partnership aimed at reviewing how Congress deals with sexual misconduct and suggesting concrete ideas for an overhaul. Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández, D-N.M., has been co-leading that effort as the chair of the Democratic Women’s Caucus alongside Republican Women’s Caucus head Kat Cammack, R-Fla.

    According to Leger Fernández, the Ethics Committee has “consulted” with her group as it weighed the changes to its internal rules.

    It has been revealed that “The Ethics Committee was clearly listening to women staffers, and has been a great partner in our work. We appreciate how they’ve consulted DWC and that these proposals will improve transparency and help protect the identities of those who report alleged misconduct. Together with RWC, we will continue to work on additional legislation in our sexual misconduct reform agenda,” she remarked in a statement earlier this week.

    Cammack said that, while “the entire system on Capitol Hill has been designed to create a chilling effect for victims,” the Ethics committee rule changes would help.

    According to recent reports, “Putting public disclosure of misconduct findings in writing, while protecting every victim’s identity, gives staffers a commitment they can count on. Faster investigations mean they get answers in time to matter,” Cammack remarked in a statement. “This is exactly the kind of change our bipartisan task force has been pushing for.”.

    Ethics ranking member Mark DeSaulnier, D-Calif., remarked everyone in the House should have “zero tolerance” for sexual harassment.

    “We’ve worked very hard to look at ways that we could make the committee’s process fair, transparent and accountable, and I think we’ve done that,” he mentioned at Thursday’s meeting.

    Latest Update: OMCO Solar offers solar-powered tracker control system

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (435 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Solarpowerworldonline

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • OMCO Solar now offers a version of its OMCO Star Tracker Control System powered entirely by solar energy, allowing tracker controls to operate without AC power at the site.
    • It has been revealed that the system, first launched last year, is designed for OMCO Origin Factory-Direct Trackers.
    • According to OMCO, the technology eliminates the need for AC power to tracker control components and an uninterruptible power supply.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    OMCO Solar now offers a version of its OMCO Star Tracker Control System powered entirely by solar energy, allowing tracker controls to operate without AC power at the site.

    It has been revealed that the system, first launched last year, is designed for OMCO Origin Factory-Direct Trackers. Its tracker controllers, array controllers and sensor bridges use all-weather battery packs charged by solar modules.

    According to OMCO, the technology eliminates the need for AC power to tracker control components and an uninterruptible power supply. It also allows tracker controls to operate and protects modules against wind, snow and hail before AC power is available.

    “Our industry has solved so many problems as we have grown – we’re now the leading source for latest electric energy capacity in the US. This addition to the OMCO Star product line solves one more – how to protect modules if there’s no AC power to the site even for a short time. We’re excited to offer this solution to our existing customers and to new partners,” said Matt Kesler, vice president of solar technology at OMCO Solar, in a statement.

    The OMCO Star system uses LoRa, or long-range, wireless technology with a communication range greater than 1 mile. According to OMCO, this reduces the number of network controllers required and allows direct communication with every tracker without relying on a mesh network.

    The firm says LoRa is 100 times less susceptible to electromagnetic noise than Zigbee and better able to connect to distant trackers despite obstacles.

    Industry observers note that OMCO says its all-weather battery packs allow the solar-powered controls to operate reliably in cold climates. The system includes field-replaceable batteries, a phone app that eliminates the need for buttons on controllers and a remote monitoring and control portal.

    The portal allows operators to move trackers for activities such as mowing, snow plowing and module cleaning. The system is developed, manufactured and supported by OMCO Solar in the United States.

    Recent findings suggest that “We are excited about bringing this innovation to the Utility Scale and DG tracker markets. Over the past few years, OMCO has expanded its capabilities beyond just being a US steel manufacturer to now being a true technology leader in our space. We look forward to supporting our customers/partners with the OMCO Star Tracker Control System, improving reliability, and reducing the labor and materials needed to build their projects,” said Eric Goodwin, vice president of business development at OMCO Solar.

    OMCO Solar will display the all-DC tracker control system at RE+ in Las Vegas, November 17–19, in the North Hall, booth N516.

    Hilton’s Cyber Week Bonus Is Worth Just $8—But You Can Stack Three Offers For 10,000 Points On A Single Night

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that hilton Honors will give you 2,000 bonus points per stay if you book by Tuesday, December 1.
    • It has been revealed that book directly with Hilton.
    • Recent findings suggest that for stays through December 31, 2026, register for More Points to Play before checkout.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that hilton Honors will give you 2,000 bonus points per stay if you book by Tuesday, December 1. I value Hilton points at 0.4 cents apiece. That’s $8 for a night at a Hampton Inn or $8 for a week at a Conrad. Book directly with Hilton. The booking window opened November 24, 2026, for stays completed November 25, 2026 through April 2, 2027. There’s no registration required or cap. (Hat tip to Head for Points.) For stays through December 31, 2026, register for More Points to Play before checkout. It adds 1,000 points at most hotels or 3,000 at listed luxury, lifestyle, resort and all-inclusive properties. With both offers that’s 3,000 points ($12) or 5,000 ($20). Award stays qualify for the fall offer. Hilton’s Cyber Week terms aren’t explicit on this but don’t exclude them. Book a Hilton Sale rate and pay the whole bill with a U.S. Hilton American Express card and you can earn another 5,000 points once per cardholder (book by December 22, stay by April 2). Book by December 1 and check out by December 31 to combine all three offers. That’s 8,000 bonus points ($32) at most hotels. At a property on the higher bonus list, one night can earn 10,000 bonus points ($40) before you count the usual hotel and card earnings. In the U.S. and Canada, the sale rate takes up to 20% off Hilton’s best available rate and requires booking at least seven days ahead. At most Hilton and Marriott brands, $100 in eligible room charges earns 1,000 base points. That’s $4 back at Hilton against about $6 at Marriott. Back in 2010, Hilton’s Jeff Diskin explained that Hilton got too little credit for what it gave every member and so promotions let them drive business. For years Hilton offered double points almost all the time. That lifted the return at most brands from 4% to 8% before elite or card bonuses.     Iran resolution blocked in first war powers vote since midterms

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (848 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Tim Kaine, D-Va., seen here at the Capitol on June 17, said additional war powers votes are under discussion for when Democrats control both chambers in the 120th Congress.
    • It has been revealed that the Senate rejected a resolution Thursday meant to rebuke President Donald Trump over the Iran war weeks after the midterm elections demonstrated the depth of public anger about the war and its effects on the U.S.
    • Senators voted 48-51 against adopting the Iran war powers resolution that the House previously adopted in mid-September that would direct the president to withdraw U.S.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., seen here at the Capitol on June 17, said additional war powers votes are under discussion for when Democrats control both chambers in the 120th Congress. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

    It has been revealed that the Senate rejected a resolution Thursday meant to rebuke President Donald Trump over the Iran war weeks after the midterm elections demonstrated the depth of public anger about the war and its effects on the U.S. economy.

    Senators voted 48-51 against adopting the Iran war powers resolution that the House previously adopted in mid-September that would direct the president to withdraw U.S. forces from the war.

    It has been revealed that as they have previously with similar measures, GOP Sens. Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska and Rand Paul of Kentucky broke with their party to support the resolution, while Democratic Sen. John Fetterman of Pennsylvania broke with his party to oppose it. Departing GOP Sens. Thom Tillis of North Carolina and Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, who have at times voted in support of similar measures, this time voted against the resolution.

    Even if the resolution was adopted in both chambers of Congress, it would be largely symbolic since, as a concurrent resolution, it would not go to the president for his signature.

    But the vote afforded senators the opportunity to register their complaints about the war for the first time since Democrats routed Republicans in the midterm elections.

    It also comes amid a larger debate within the Democratic Party on how best to fulfill their campaign promise of ending the war as they prepare to take control of Congress next year.

    It has been revealed that democrats have become increasingly interested in trying to cut off funding for the war rather than continuing to hold war powers votes. But they are divided on whether to demand an immediate end to funding in the next government funding bill in December or to wait until they take power in January.

    Industry observers note that “When we have the gavels, we are contemplating other things, and we're actually contemplating things in connection with the CR discussion,” Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., told reporters Thursday in an apparent reference to the debate among Democrats.

    According to recent reports, as of Nov. 13, the war has cost at least $48.3 billion, up from $47 billion last month, the nominee to be Navy comptroller, Arthur Miller, told the Senate Armed Services Committee at his confirmation hearing Thursday.

    As with previous estimates, the number Miller cited Thursday includes munitions, equipment replacement costs and operational costs but does not factor in the cost of damage to U.S. bases, which alone is likely to run in the billions.

    Last week, a trio of Senate Democrats unveiled legislation to prohibit funding for offensive military operations in Iran that they noted they intend to introduce as an amendment to the next government funding bill, which Congress will need to pass to avoid a government shutdown after Dec. 11.

    Recent findings suggest that on Thursday as the Senate voted on the war powers resolution, Sens. Tammy Duckworth, D-Ill., and Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y., two of the sponsors of the proposed amendment, demanded it be included in the next funding bill.

    Industry observers note that “We’ve already tried tool after tool to get the president to rein in this conflict. Nine months in, defunding the war is the only way to force Trump to end it,” Duckworth, who vowed to vote against any continuing resolution that doesn’t include the amendment, remarked at a news conference.

    Recent findings suggest that sen. Michael Bennet, D-Colo., unveiled his own proposed amendment Thursday to bar any future and previous funding from being used to “support directly or indirectly combat activities by United States personnel in or over Iran, or in Iranian territorial waters” unless specifically authorized by Congress.

    His legislation is modeled off of language Congress passed in 1973 to cut off funding for the Nixon administration’s bombing campaign in Cambodia, Bennet’s office said in a news release.

    Sources indicate that “When we vote on short-term spending in the near future, we can fund the government and end this war. It is what the American people demand, and what they deserve,” Bennet said in a statement.

    Meanwhile, the House is likely to vote again on a war powers resolution before year’s end.

    “Before the lame duck’s over, I hope to enforce a war powers resolution vote, and it’ll be a chance for Republicans to say whether they did or didn’t get the message on Nov. 3,” Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., mentioned Thursday in a brief interview, referring to the date of the elections.

    Sources indicate that as with previous resolutions, Massie’s would direct the president to remove U.S. military units from hostilities against Iran unless specifically authorized by Congress or needed to defend against an imminent attack.

    The resolution was filed Nov. 10, and under the 1973 War Powers Resolution, Massie can force a vote 15 calendar days after its introduction.

    John M. Donnelly and Lauren Green contributed to this report.

    #169859. Gratitude Is the Taproot of American Identity

    📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (244 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Nationalreview ↗ Open Full Page

    Gratitude Is the Taproot of American Identity

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (244 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Nationalreview

    ⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Gratitude is like stretching, or deep breathing, or drinking water.
    • In a recent development, but then of course — like drinking water, or breathing deeply — giving thanks is also something you’re always glad you did.
    • Klavan is the associate editor of the Claremont Review of Books and a professor of classical literature at the University of Austin.

    Gratitude is like stretching, or deep breathing, or drinking water. It’s one of those miraculous things you can do for free, any time, with barely any effort, and it’s 100 percent certain to make you feel better — but somehow practicing it always feels like an exasperating chore. That’s how I experience it, anyway. There comes a moment at nearly all Thanksgiving tables when someone says, Now let’s all go around and say one thing we’re thankful for. And when this unimpeachably virtuous ritual is confirmed, my first thought is always, Oh God, when will it be over?

    In a recent development, but then of course — like drinking water, or breathing deeply — giving thanks is also something you’re always glad you did. Lo and behold, there really are people and things you love in this world, and to make a point of looking on them with appreciation is to see them lit up again in the living color of your own happiness. You might start out by dragging your feet; you are guaranteed to end up flush with joy. Maybe that’s part of the point: It changes you inside.

    Spencer A. Klavan is the associate editor of the Claremont Review of Books and a professor of classical literature at the University of Austin. His new book, A Way With Words: Why Language Makes Humans Irreplaceable, is available for preorder now.

    On “Gratitude Is the Taproot of American Identity”.

    American Airlines and Citi are working on a $695 AAdvantage Executive card for small businesses. It’s been an odd omission. The $695 United Club Business Card already earns 1.5 miles per dollar on everyday spending. Delta Air Lines has its $650 SkyMiles Reserve Business card. American’s Admirals Club card has been a consumer product.

    It has been revealed that doctor of Credit shares some card designs that Citi is surveying. One looks a lot like the consumer Citi® / AAdvantage® Executive World Legend Mastercard® [See rates and fees] I’ve carried for a long time. However, the other would earn: 1.5 miles and 1.5 Loyalty Points per dollar on everyday purchases. Put $100,000 of bills on one employee’s card in a qualification year and the business would earn 150,000 redeemable miles. The employee would earn 150,000 Loyalty Points, enough for Platinum Pro, and the owner would earn 100,000 Loyalty Points, enough for Platinum. In January I wrote about Citi testing a $150 fee for the regular business card and the idea of replacing its $99 companion certificate with a flight discount. Citi went ahead with the fee and kept the certificate. So not everything being tested happens, and I’d put the strongest prediction on a card like this coming at a $695 annual fee with Admirals Club membership, realizing that the rest are potential options under consideration (and in some cases even controls that aren’t going to make the final product). Credit: Doctor of Credit What The Lounge Membership Gets A Business Both versions give the primary cardmember Admirals Club membership with up to two guests. The personal card also admits immediate family, which matters when there are four (or more) of you. Employee cards carry no additional annual fee. The organization can buy lounge access for the people who travel, at $175 total for the first three and $175 apiece after that. So that’s basically the same as the consumer card, except that the annual fee plus lounge is optional rather. American charges $1,200 to $1,400 for full membership, depending on status. And the clubs are getting better. I prefer the newer American lounges to what United and Delta are building. My home club in Austin is slated to double in size and get an outdoor terrace. Someone who wants the lounge may already have gotten the Citi® / AAdvantage® Executive World Legend Mastercard®. But Citi’s going to want the smaller group of customers who want major company expenses on a business account. Some Ideas Being Surveyed For The Card Both versions shared from this survey would earn 4 miles per dollar on American Airlines and 12 on eligible hotel and car bookings through American. Both come with Group 4 boarding, priority check-in and screening, Omni Champion and Avis President’s Club status, up to $100 for inflight or club purchases, and $15 in Lyft credit after three eligible rides in a month. One largely copies the personal Executive card. It earns one mile and one Loyalty Point per dollar on ordinary spending, plus 10,000 Loyalty Points at each of four balances (50,000, 90,000, 165,000 and 240,000). The other awards 1.5 Loyalty Points on every eligible dollar the cardholder spends. It drops the four milestones, along with the two $250 American Airlines Vacations credits and two $100 inKind dining credits. Instead there’s $20 a month toward Melio or Xero and half off an annual Fox One and Wall Street Journal bundle (meh). It adds Sixt to the $120 Avis and Budget credit and covers a second domestic checked bag. But its two Omni free nights interest me. On the personal Executive card you enroll and complete a qualifying stay of at least two consecutive nights booked directly with Omni to earn one free night. If this didn’t require a stay to earn that would be exceptionally valuable (I’d probably redeem them in New York or worst case if I didn’t otherwise use them, down the street at Barton Creek Resort in Austin). I like the potential add-on of rewards for $100,000 in spending, since the consumer version doesn’t really give a strong incentive to actually spend money on the card (it’s a great one to get and keep, but spending is really only incentivized by the Loyalty Points). Here they’re surveying a choice of 2,500 Loyalty Points, two Flagship Lounge passes or a $200 flight discount. American sells the passes for $150 apiece, though I’d value them as an upgrade from the Admirals Club I can already visit. It’s probably best to just take the flight discount unless the points pushed someone over a status or reward threshold. The $200 adds just 0.2% across $100,000. But for someone already at $96,000 spend it’s worthwhile for the next $4,000. Would I Keep Two $695 American Airlines Cards? I have the regular Citi® / AAdvantage BusinessTM World Elite Mastercard® [See rates and fees], and there’s a reason to spend on it even at one mile per dollar. Through December 31, 2028, eligible purchases on an employee’s card earn a Loyalty Point for the employee and another for the primary cardmember. Both survey designs call that a promotion. On the more interesting version of the premium business card, the extra half Loyalty Point goes to the person whose name is on the card. If employees pay the bills, the owner’s rate on those purchases stays at one. An owner who earns all four personal Executive bonuses from flying could give up 40,000 Loyalty Points by replacing the personal card with that one. The regular business card’s fee goes from $99 to $150 on January 24, 2027. At $100,000 of ordinary spending, E would cost $545 more and earn 50,000 more redeemable miles. That’s 1.09 cents per extra mile before valuing Omni nights or other benefits. If the alternative is a 2% cash back card with no annual fee, though, you’re giving up $2,000 and paying $695.     📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The new state-of-the-art factory in Oklahoma City will create about 300 jobs, strengthen the domestic solar supply chain, and establish a new benchmark for transparency and quality.

    This month, Nextnova celebrated the official inauguration of its latest solar cell manufacturing facility in Oklahoma City, marking an important milestone in strengthening America’s domestic solar manufacturing industry.

    The facility will manufacture high-efficiency solar cells using advanced automation, Industry 4.0 technologies, and comprehensive digital traceability.

    Production is scheduled to begin in March 2027 with an initial annual capacity of 2 GW, designed to expand to 5 GW as market demand grows.

    According to recent reports, the latest factory is expected to create approximately 300 skilled jobs in engineering, manufacturing, quality assurance, and operations, supporting economic growth while reinforcing the U.S. clean energy supply chain.

    Nextnova celebrates the inauguration of its upcoming solar cell manufacturing facility in Oklahoma City. Credit: Nextnova.

    Sources indicate that “Today represents an exciting milestone for Nextnova and for American solar manufacturing,” noted Nathan Kii Miller, Nextnova’s chief strategy officer, in a statement. “Our Oklahoma City facility combines advanced manufacturing technology, complete supply chain transparency, and rigorous quality standards to deliver premium solar cells while strengthening a resilient domestic solar industry.”.

    Designed for maximum quality and reliability, the facility features fully integrated manufacturing execution systems (MES), automated inspection technologies, advanced process control, and a dedicated analytical laboratory supporting continuous quality verification throughout production.

    Nextnova notes that its commitment to transparent sourcing, manufacturing excellence, and scalable production provides customers with high-performance solar cells that support the continued growth of a secure and competitive U.S. solar industry.

    I’ve had first hand reports of this as well – the Trump administration has been refusing ESTAs to former U.S. citizens, requiring a full visa, even when they are citizens of and residing in visa waiver countries. The fact alone that they are ex-citizens keeps them from a smooth visit path, independent of any risk factors, and even if they’ve visited using ESTAs for 15 years.

    This is a big deal for anyone thinking about renouncing US citizenship.

    Sources indicate that many assume they can keep visiting the US after renunciation on ESTA based on their other citizenship. But there are more and more reports of former citizens being denied ESTA and told to apply for a visitor visa instead.

    According to recent reports, A visitor visa, unlike ESTA, generally requires a consular interview and proving that the applicant will leave after the visit. With family, businesses, or assets in the US, that could mean delays and refusals. This has to factor into the decision on whether or not to renounce.

    Van Hollen: Senate rules changes a matter for caucus to decide

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (558 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., during a press conference on Thursday.
    • Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., endorsed a bipartisan plan Thursday to adopt new rules aimed at speeding up Senate procedures but stopped short of calling for abolishing the filibuster, laying down a marker on a key internal debate for Democrats as he positions himself to challenge Senate Minority Leader Charles E.
    • Sources indicate that van Hollen joined Sen.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that sen. Jeff Merkley, D-Ore. looks on as Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., during a press conference on Thursday. (Finn Gomez/Getty Images).

    Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., endorsed a bipartisan plan Thursday to adopt new rules aimed at speeding up Senate procedures but stopped short of calling for abolishing the filibuster, laying down a marker on a key internal debate for Democrats as he positions himself to challenge Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y.

    Sources indicate that van Hollen joined Sen. Jeff Merkley, D-Ore., at a press conference Thursday to express his support for a initiative from Merkley and Sen. Steve Daines, R-Mont., to, among other changes, adopt a “talking filibuster,” requiring senators to continuously hold the floor if they seek to prevent a bill or nomination from moving forward.

    Van Hollen went further to say that while his personal view is that the filibuster itself is “anti-democratic,” changes beyond what Merkley and Daines are proposing are a matter for further discussion.

    “I’m in favor of filibuster reform,” Van Hollen remarked. “How and when we do that is a matter for the caucus to decide.”.

    The filibuster, a Senate tactic that effectively requires a 60-vote threshold to advance most legislation, has long been the subject of calls for change or outright abolition from members of both parties.

    Other changes Merkley and Daines unveiled in October include eliminating cloture requirements for nominations and amendments, reducing post-cloture time for legislation, and introducing a latest suspension process modeled after the House rules to allow bills with broad support to move swiftly.

    Merkley actually held two separate press conferences Thursday on his filibuster proposal, one with his Montana Republican co-sponsor and then later with Van Hollen, whose bid to become majority leader he has endorsed.

    At the earlier appearance, Daines mentioned that he thought the changes, if adopted, would “truly be a cultural change for the Senate” and lead to greater bipartisanship.

    “We believe these reforms are appropriate no matter who is in the majority, no matter what the election outcomes were,” Daines said.

    Daines also reiterated his view that implementing any rules changes would require 67 votes from the full chamber.

    But Democrats have been debating whether to use their upcoming majority in 2027 to change the rules on the first day of the session with 51 votes, or to eventually employ the so-called “nuclear option,” a series of procedural moves leading to a simple majority vote.

    Sources indicate that democrats used that tool in 2013 to lower the voting threshold for advancing some presidential nominations with a simple majority, rather than 60 votes. A Republican majority followed in 2017 by extending that change to include Supreme Court nominations, and again in 2019 to reduce the number of hours between a cloture and final confirmation vote.

    A spokesperson for Schumer declined to comment on Van Hollen’s endorsement of the Merkley-Daines strategy.

    Schumer has mentioned he remains confident in his bid to remain party leader.

    Van Hollen reiterated Thursday that his “momentum is growing,” after several senators-elect have thrown their support behind the Maryland Democrat.

    “I think people recognize that if we're going to deliver on the massive things that the American voters stood up for and voted for, you can't just go back to business as usual and status quo,” Van Hollen remarked.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Southwest Airlines will give you a Companion Pass for a single holiday roundtrip, even if you book the cheapest Basic fare with points. From January 8 through March 3, 2027, you can bring someone on as many trips as you like for just the taxes and fees (from $5.60 each way). You can use points for your seat then, too.

    In a recent development, register for the Black Friday offer first, then book by 11:59 p.m. Central on Sunday, November 29. Put your Rapid Rewards number on the reservation when you book.

    It has been revealed that already booked for Christmas? If the same award or paid ticket still costs the same, then register, cancel and rebook. And for a winter trip where you’ll use the pass, you can book your seat now and add your companion once the pass is active, as long as there’s still a seat for sale.

    Southwest gets your Christmas booking this weekend and gives you the second seat after the holiday rush. If you earned the pass they offered in August, yours starts January 5 and also ends March 3. This offer adds zero days. You get one designated companion at a time across all your passes, with three changes for 2027 after you pick the first person.

    I used to buy my ticket, bring my wife as my companion and redeem points for our daughter. With two kids, I’d register both parents. Each can earn a pass and designate a child. If one parent already earned August’s pass, only the other needs to qualify this time. Fly Austin to Orlando and back nonstop in February and the two kids’ tickets together would cost $22.40 in taxes and fees, even if both parents use points.

    Sources indicate that this year it takes 135,000 Companion Pass qualifying points or 100 qualifying one-way flights to earn the full pass. Under the Rapid Rewards changes for 2027, unlimited companion travel comes with Platinum status starting January 1. That takes the same 100 flights – or 140,000 tier qualifying points. At 75 flights or 95,000 tier qualifying points you get three companion trips, each of which can be a roundtrip. What made the old pass so easy to earn was that a credit card initial bonus could cover most of those 135,000 points.     📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Southwest Airlines’ Companion Pass, which allows you to bring a friend nearly for free (you just have to pay the taxes and fees) on unlimited flights, is one of the most valuable assets in the world of points and miles.

    It normally takes a whole lot of flying to unlock this pass — and one of the popular shortcuts that allows you to earn this pass with points from Southwest credit card bonuses is ending soon, which will only make it even harder to earn.

    Recent findings suggest that but if you'd rather spend your Black Friday weekend booking flights than buying discounted sweatpants, there is some good news. There's a new limited-time opportunity to earn a promotional Southwest Companion Pass if you book one round-trip or two one-way eligible Southwest flights by Sunday, Nov. 29, 2026, and travel on those flights by Jan. 5, 2027.

    Your promotional Companion Pass would then be valid for unlimited use between Jan. 8, 2027, and March 3, 2027.

    First, register for the promotion with your Southwest Rapid Rewards number. Then, book one qualifying round-trip flight or two one-way flights using your Rapid Rewards number by 11:59 p.m. CST on Sunday, Nov. 29. Flights must be completed sometime from Nov. 27 to Jan. 5, 2027.

    Successfully complete the above steps, and you'll earn a promotional Companion Pass valid for use between Jan. 8 and March 3, 2027.

    All fare classes, including the carrier’s Basic option, are eligible for this promotion. And it doesn’t matter how you pay for your flight, as there's no specific spending requirement. Rapid Rewards point redemptions and Cash + Points bookings qualify too, as long as you book through Southwest channels, such as the carrier’s website or mobile app.

    If you have existing flights on Southwest, they won't automatically count for this promotion. However, if you can cancel those reservations, register and rebook before the promotion ends on Sunday, that should work (provided you complete your travel within the qualifying travel window). Be sure to check for any fare differences before canceling.

    Southwest’s Companion Pass is almost legendary in the world of points and miles. It lets you bring a companion along on unlimited flights, whether you book with cash or points, for almost free. As long as there’s an open seat on the plane, your companion can fly with you for just the cost of taxes and fees (which start at $5.60).

    According to recent reports, you must designate a companion in your Rapid Rewards account. However, you’re allowed to change your designated companion up to three times per year, and this rule applies to promotional passes as well.

    If you'd like to earn a Companion Pass for longer than just eight weeks or so this promotional pass is valid, there is still time to earn a Companion Pass for all of 2027 using the welcome bonuses from the Southwest credit cards as outlined here. You have to act rapidly, though, since those rules are changing soon.

    Related: Best Southwest Airlines credit cards.

    The Southwest Companion Pass can be extremely valuable for those who like to travel with a companion. Earning one is about to become a lot harder, so this is a great promotion for those who can register, book eligible travel by Sunday and travel between now and Jan. 5, 2027.
